If you're looking for your first 3d printer don't buy this one. I finished assembling mine and it worked well for two days until the thermistor went bad in the heat bed. And I'm not even mentioning the bolt I had to retap or parts that weren't quite right out of the box. The thing is if you want a 3d printer that works as a 3d printer buy a premade one first.

If you're looking for a fun project, then assembling and modifying this is pretty fun, but this won't work for very long out of the box. It can be fixed and made more reliable, but if it stops working, you wont' be able to 3d print any replacement parts or modifications. If you're excited to try 3d printing, you'll be turned away at a product like this.

all of that aside the working product is okay without any mods, however you can tell that the micro controller in it is very laggy on the button presses. I have to push the buttons 2 or 3 times before it registers. the firmware must not check for button presses frequently enough. that's just bad programming. in my case where the thermistor went bad, it was had to diagnose since both the temperatures came up with an error even though one sensor was working perfectly. again just bad coding, it should still display the working temperature reading even if it won't print.

I don't regret my purchase because I like engineering and I like to solve problems. this printer has a lot of problems to solve if you want a really good 3d printer. So what I'm saying is this is a good purchase for people who like to design things and want a starting point to improve off of, but if you're wanting a 3d printer buy something that is premade because the quality is so hit or miss on these kits.

I bought this exact same diamond grinding cup in January from a local big box store (Lowes). I used it to grind down a 13’ x 15’ concrete floor to prepare it for a permeating sealer. I also used it to remove a bunch of self leveling and regular concrete on the pool decking along with removing old thin set on an 3’ x 8’ knee wall. The wheel that I used for all of that stuff was getting pretty low so I decided to quick order another one here so I didn’t have to go to the store and waste time.

When this new cup arrived I didn’t think anything was off, the packaging looked normal so I just assumed it was a genuine product. Once I started using it I couldn’t believe how much it was ‘checking’ and wanted to just pull the grinder all over the place. I dismissed it thinking that once it wears into my grove it will be fine. It eased up a bit on the checking, but the pulling didn’t and was consistent from start to finish.

This wasn’t a big project, but ended up taking all day because this cup just couldnt cut through it very well. (This was a 3’ x 10’ area w/ around 1/2” - 3/4” thin set on it to be removed.) As another person commented you couldnt create a smooth finish because it left grooves on the surface. This cup also wore down quickly and 3/4 the way through the job it started bogging my Bosch grinder.

I decided to switched back to the old cup that I bought back in January. Lo and behold the old cup cut through everything like butter! There wasn’t any checking, pulling or grooves. I ended up going over everything I did earlier to fix it and make it look right.

When I changed out the cups I noticed how the paint was coming off the one I just got, so I decided to compare the two even closer ~ side by side. Not only did the paint start coming off, but it was a different color. Same thing with the identifying product numbers on it, a completely different color! The base of the cup is also slightly different and the material just doesn’t feel the same. The product packaging looks like it may be authentic, but thats about as far as it goes with this thing.

Now here’s my gripe... I can understand using a cheap tool if it really doesn’t matter, but you NEVER buy a cheap/knockoff grinding wheel because you dont know how well that wheel is going to hold up to the extreme speed/force that its under. If part of the wheel were to break or splinter off it could seriously hurt or kill someone. I chose a name brand product thinking I was getting a quality name brand product, not some knockoff pos! If that was the route I was going for I could’ve spent a lot less and got the same quality item.

I am the type of person who never leaves negative feedback but in this case I must. Despite how easy to use they make the product look in the video, this kit was very frustrating and ultimately a complete waste of time and money. Like the instructions say, to tighten the nuts you insert a wrench in between the two nuts and tighten until secure. Then you remove the second top nut with the wrench leaving the first, bottom nut on the backside of the post. The problem is, when adequately tightened, the second nut is so securely set against the first that when you back the second one off, the first nut comes with it and the whole assembly loosens up again. And thanks to the anti-tamper feature of the bolt head, you can't use a screwdriver to keep it from spinning when you try to remove it. Ultimately I had to use an angle grinder to remove the spinning bolts and it marred the finish on my sign. No chance of getting a refund now. Don't waste your money. Find another way.

This is functional with some constant manipulation from the user to keep it going - in hindsight would have bought something different and paid more for something better - will buy something that works properly now and keep this "pain in the butt to use" one as a back-up emergency unit.

Why:
1st - the bags they sell together with the unit from amazon are too big to fit on the spindle so you have to unroll half of the bags and feed them manually (waste of time). The reason is the design of the unit, look at most competitors, the part that holds the bags is in the far rear, not off-set to the side, which makes the opening to feed the bags too small, and the roll of bags wont fit on the spindle on the sealer unit.

2nd - the unit continuity mis feeds and the bags get stuck and melt so you have to un jam the unit (it happens so frequently you can not blink or have it run without having to keep your hands there to pull the bags properly to feed. I've run through 2 rolls of bags - same thing - it's so labor intensive it's labor intensive it's not worth the time - you'd be better off buying bags already blown up and spend your time doing other things).

3rd -the warm up time is about 6-8 minutes compared to other machines with a shorter warm up time.

4th - the air pump in this specific machine is not strong enough to fill larger bags - the air flow in to the bags does not provide enough volume of air to fill it before the bag before it becomes sealed by the machine (making the bag 100% useless - they only half fill - so expect to throw away any large bag roll you buy or you need to purchase a 2nd machine that can actually fill them).

5th - It gets stuck so much you have to stop everything, adjust the roll, and reset the roll on the air fill tube - it takes a few minutes, so a lot of wasted time using this machine.

Do yourself a favor and spend the money now on a better solution!

There are some cool things about this set, but now that I’ve been using it I don’t think there are any benefits that outweigh the oddities that would be eliminated by just buying a typical slanting knife block set.

Because this stands upright rather than at an angle, it can’t hold what I would refer to as a “watermelon knife” (a knife long enough to slice through a watermelon). It also only comes with 4 matching steak knives rather than a full set of 8.

I’m 5’2” and I didn’t realize how important that slanted angle is until having to look straight on at this block. The knives therefore look cluttered from my angle. Plus, it feels much more natural to pull a knife towards me rather than straight up. This also means that it can’t be stored under a kitchen cabinet.

As you can see, the block separates into 2 parts in a unique way. I can’t think of a scenario in which this would be helpful.

Got my printer from amazon back in august because it was readily available and at the solidoodle site was a couple of weeks out. Printer arrived, set it up and started playing with it. Temperature readings off the extruder would start flickering and dropping a up to 50C instantaneously.

Here is why the 1 star rating: no support whatsoever from solidoodle. And poor quality.

I thought I had a problem with the model or something else, so I tried to contact then via email. No response in over 10 days. Tried calling them, left message, no reply in over a week. And here is the kicker: Since I thought I needed parts, was browsing parts over the solidoodle site to see what I might need, and I placed a couple of things on my cart, but never checked out. The very next morning I get an email form Daniel, asking me if there was an issue that prevented me to complete my order.... seriously???? I've been waiting for a response for a week, but if you try to buy something then you DO get a response.... interesting......

Never the less, I took the machine apart and one of the leads off the thermistor was broken, replaced the part with a new connector and seems liek everything is working fine. Still need to try to print this big part and see if something else craps out.

If you are ok with no support and are a DIY type of person, purchase form this guys. Otherwise stay away.

This printer is touted as being a printer to teach your kids how to 3D print. I embarrassed to say I thought this would be a fairly easy way to learn from if it was for kids.

I have an IT background so the concept of 3D printing I understood but I have “ZERO” experience in 3D printing. I will just list the things I didn’t like than the things I did.

The literature. Most of what is explained from the manual was easy enough to understand. It was also equally as easy to understand from the printer display.

Another example is the glue stick and all the tools that came with the printer, which were quite a few, nowhere could I find in the literature anything that describes what you are to use these items for or why you have them. I had to go to YouTube video to figure out why I was given a glue stick from somebody who had explained the magic of using a Glue stick for 3D printing. The reason you need the glue stick is to help keep your print jobs from breaking free from the magnetic print plate.

I couldn’t understand why some of the things I wanted to print would print the Adhesion print base and others wouldn’t. Again my original problem was getting the jobs to stick to the plate needing the glue stick.

After eight print jobs the Zero leveling stopped working now I can’t print anything.

Another issue we had was filament. Again referring to my number one complaint about the tech manual I didn’t see anything that said don’t do these things. As an example. Don’t let the filament run out otherwise it will be hard as the dickens to feed more filament into the printer when you do get more PLA filament. Also with the filament, I didn’t see anything that said, especially on the side of the printer, that “This size of spool” will only fit this feed arm. Instead there is a nice picture of how you are to feed the filament into the feeder and when you go to Amazon to buy a spools of PLA filament all the spools look like the picture. Afterwards when you get it, “surprise” it doesn’t fit and won’t work unless you manually feed it off the spool and keep an eye on it so it doesn’t get tangled up. I just recently saw on Youtube a gentleman who also reviewed this product said it would have been nice to come with a spool holder because most filament spools where the size that he had and consequently so did I.

Wireless. You have to use your phone with a downloaded App (Polo Print) to provide a wireless connection for your printer to connect to the internet. Why?? I found no way at all to get it to map to your home network like a regular printer.

There were only three ways I can see to get your print jobs to the printer:

Connect it directly to your computer. It is small and takes up a small footprint but if your desk/work area is already short on desktop real-estate then it will not work. Even if you could sit it on your desk it is “loud and noisy” and if you have a print job that is going to take up to 18 hours that is too much noise.
SD mem card. It comes with a USB thumb drive adapter. It works but it is on the cheesy side. I always felt like I was putting it in wrong even when I knew I was putting it incorrectly.

Cloud printing. HOWEVER, you had to use the POLO Print App.

What I liked:

When it worked it worked well. I printed 8 objects twice. Out of the 8, only two turned out. One was a figurine and the Other SCI-FI piece. The others didn’t turn out, I wasn’t doing anything different from the ones that did work except on the two pieces I tried printing twice I tried a finer layer height.

The Cura 4.3.0 software. I Loved this software! It made pulling a 3D print and editing it to be sliced for printing at least that much easier to understand.

Users devoted to the Dyson seem to be under some magical spell. My mother and my daughter both love Dyson along with many other friends and acquaintances. I bought the Animal Upright after hearing a variety of people rave about their Dyson. I was first surprised by the flimsy construction of some of the plastic parts. You must be gentle as my mom discovered after letting my dad do the vacuuming one day. He broke a part that moves to empty the canister.
Speaking of the canister, it is very small. If you have pets like this vacuum is supposedly designed for, you should expect to empty the canister at least once for any large rug that a pet spends a lot of time on. I am not a fan of bagless vacuums in general since they all generate a poof a dust as they are emptied, but the Dyson is worse than most because the area that collects debris is like a small ring around the outside of the canister. We have a long haired dog and the debris will not just fall out if you let it fill up to the fill line. Dirt, hair and wool must be pulled free by hand with the use of a wire or chopstick. Not a pleasant experience.
It is also extremely difficult to use the hand tools with this vacuum. The hose comes out near the top of the handle and is nice and long, but you need one hand on the vacuum to hold it in place and keep the hose from going back in while you use the other hand to clean. Otherwise the vacuum drags around every time you move the hose around. I will never purchase another Dyson product.

its rated at 110 volts AC, 3000 watts, 3000/110 = 27 amps. Most home 120 volts AC outlets are 15 amp rated, and the kitchen is 20 amps. thankfully they have rewired the thing so it will never reach 27 amps, but in doing so they may have cut the performance in half. (yup, confirmed) In addition, they didnt put on the power cord strain relief, so it can be easily yanked out if your not careful. I measured my unit, at 120 volts AC plug voltage, I measured 14 amps, 120 X 14 = 1680 watts. Not safe for anything but the 20 amp kitchen outlets, even better if its on its own power line.
Bottom line, this thing is not safe to plug into any shared kitchen outlet that would allow the circuit to exceed 20 amps, the power cord is not safe with the strain relief missing, and since you are only putting in half the energy 1680 watts instead of 3000 watts, it will probably never get up to temperature, or cook properly. (yup, confirmed below)

I spent 15 or 20 minutes with assorted knives, tweezers, and scraping tools trying to unravel the loose end of the first roll I tried.

Take a look at the dispenser for an ordinary roll of Scotch Tape. See the little porch to support the loose end and the serrated teeth to cut a length? THATS what this product should have. It would cost pennies.

I managed to get the loose end on the second roll. The first will end up in the trash. A simple but effective plastic clip identifying the loose end and securing it, would make all the difference. Other manufactures do it better.

Perhaps the industrial chemists could come up with a preservative that is not. Sodium Carbonate (aka Washing soda) or Sodium Citrate are nontoxic in small amounts. First off, I am a newbie when it comes to 3D printing so I am still figuring out what makes a print great. For this reason, I typically would not rate this product just yet, but I just bought this brand of white PLA after using HATCHBOX PLA in white since 2018 and I am seeing a big difference in the two products so figured I could do more of a comparison review.

HATCHBOX is a true white, whereas the SUNLU is a bit off-white.
HATCHBOX printed a box, on the first attempt, with no warping. I am on my third attempt to print the same box using SUNLU, the first two attempts warped so I am having to get creative.

I have a non-heated, glass print-bed and use the blue painter's tape and a glue stick for most of my prints with no issues. In this third attempt at the box, I am using CCTREE 3D Printer Build Surface that has an adhesive back and glue. I may have to try hairspray if warping occurs again. So far I much prefer HATCHBOX PLA over SUNLU PLA. Though time and trial will only tell if the warping is more user error or PLA error.

Like many other reviewers here, I had over half of these break the tips off as I attempted to get them into the dry wall. No there were no studs behind them.

I was careful, tried pre-drilling and screwing by hand to not over-torque them. I think I know why these happen - I noticed these are made in China, and from my experience having our products manufactured over there, it's very common for the factories to make tiny adjustments that they don't their customer about, to use less material in order to save a tiny amount of money on raw material costs. I can only assume that in this particular case, the material is cheaper and the thickness has been reduced right to the borderline of not-working to lower the amount of material required to make.

It's frustrating - the tips break, and you have use needle-nose pliers to extradite them and attempt again. A couple just tore up the drywall to the point of usability. The jobs I did took much longer than they should have to install. When they do work, they work ok - much better than plastic anchors, but I question the claimed 50 pound rating.

Okay, I’m docking these down from three stars to one star, because for the past 4 months, I have been receiving multiple emails from people I believe are associated with the seller, asking me to delete my originally 3-starred review. For a few weeks, I was getting these emails DAILY. I absolutely refuse to delete my review, and contacted Amazon community and customer support multiple times in regards to this situation. They didn't seem to be able to resolve the issue, because the emails continued until I finally replied to one telling them to "F off." The emails stopped for a few weeks after that, but they're at it again. ORIGINAL REVIEW:
I purchased these in the beginning of February, to wear under my cloth masks at work. They work fine. They're breathable, the elastic has a good amount of give to it without being too loose, and the wire on the top helps give you a more snug fit around your face. (If you wear glasses, the wire really helps prevent your glasses from fogging up.)

Regardless of the fit and ease of wearing these while double masking at work, it's the smell that I can't get over. I unpackaged all 100 masks the day they came in, and they have been spread out on my dresser airing out ever since. It's been well over a month now, and yet they STILL have this weird smell to them. I'm not sure what it is; it's sort of a chemical smell, probably from the materials used or the packaging, I don't know.

The smell does go away for the most part once you hang them up somewhere individually for 2-3 days. (I hang mine near an air vent so they get some more air circulation.) Unfortunately, I don't have enough space to hang up 100 individual masks simultaneously, so I just hang up 2-3 at a time, letting them air out by the vent for a couple days before I have to wear them. I would assume hanging them up on a clothesline or something outside might do the trick, and if it wasn't the height of pollen allergy season, I might give that a go.

As it is, the smell is a huge inconvenience that outweighs the pros of these masks. If you've got the time and space to air all these masks out before using them, they're worth a shot, but personally, I will not be ordering these again.

I've been using Hatchbox PLA and ABS for awhile now. This is the 4th spool of Hatchbox I've purchased, and may possibly be the last. The first 3 spools ran fine, but the winding on this spool was off. On first observation, everything looked great! The winding was tight and orderly. Issues arose after my first print with this spool when it failed mid-print due to the winding being off and overlapping, causing the extruder to not be able to unwind the PLA. This was bad for me as I do very large prints, often taking 11+ hours to complete. Nobody wants to babysit a large print, but this spool would require that. I attempted a 2nd print, having loosened the winding on the Hatchbox spool, but this still failed mid-print as the spool had countless revolutions and was able to catch up to the point I had loosened too, causing another failed print. Approximately 12 hours of printing wasted, on 2 separate attempts, and about 40 meters of PLA wasted.

This may seem to others like a one off issue, but having a 25% failure rate of Hatchbox spools certainly does not leave a good taste in my mouth. I cannot return this spool as I am well outside the return window for Amazon, and it is only a $22 loss for me, but I am very nervous running my remaining Hatchbox spools at this point.

Be warned, if the winding is tight you may encounter the same issue I've had. I've given a 1 star review as this spool is unusable to me at this point. Adhesion and warmth are good quality, but that is worthless if the printer cannot unwind the spool without constant assistance!

Still, I had a set of leads so I decided to just cut off the shrouds to see if that would work.  The 8012A has a 2 ohm resistance scale.  I tried to zero out the resistance of the leads but no dice.  To make a long story short, these probes are made with number 36 wire!!! Each lead had half an ohm of resistance.  So, if you are going to measure voltage, current only amounting to a few milliamps, and don't care if you get a large error in measuring low values of resistance, then this set is for you.  Otherwise I would avoid it like the plague.

I've used Hatchbox PLA filament for a few years and generally been pleased with the results. I bought two spools of the Gray Filament in December and just loaded them onto my Ender 3 and Qidi Tech 1 printers. I was having issues with a 0.2mm Nozzle on the Qidi Tech so I installed a 0.4mm and noticed similar issues. I also noticed similar under extrusion issues on the Ender 3. After some trial and error with print settings, I finally measured the filament diameter since nothing was resolving my issues. The diameter of the filament is anywhere between 1.66mm and 1.70mm - at no point in measuring along multiple lengths of filament did I find it to be 1.75mm. If you assume their dimensional accuracy is from 1.75mm, this is no where close to the advertised +/- 0.03mm. The filament I used immediately preceding this filament was a Zibo Marble PLA and the quality of that compared to the Hatchbox was leaps and bounds better.

With the increased cost of USPS Priority Mail shipping, I was looking for a way to cut some costs. I came across these 14x6x2 boxes and the dimensions of this box exactly falls in the 0.1 cubic feet USPS Priority Mail shipping tier. The boxes I've been using have been 14x4x4 and 14x6x4 and are in the 0.2 cubic feet tier (which is almost $1 more than 0.1 cubic feet from California to the East Coast where most of my customers are) so I was excited to find this 14x6x2 box here on Amazon. The vendors I buy boxes from don't carry this size.

2-stars for the box size but that's where the stars end. The cardboard used for these boxes, sadly, are quite thin. I only use ECT-32 to keep the weight down and what I ship isn't exactly fragile but with enough force, is breakable. Comparing all the ECT-32 boxes I've been using from a well known box vendor, these 14x6x2 boxes feel MUCH MUCH flimsier than those. The corrugated middle layer easily compresses when I barely pinch my thumb and index finger against it. REALLY REALLY cheap quality.

Unless you're shipping anything that absolutely won't break -- like a stack of paper or fabric -- look elsewhere! You've been warned!

UPDATE:
I attempted to ship an item with this box anyways and after taping up the box, I was able to crush the edge of the box with one hand without a lot of force. Introduction: I do not print any models, decorative elements and so on. I only print functional parts, such as levers, gears, angles, adapters, screws, etc. So all my info below is based on my experience in that field. Honestly, I don't know or care how another anime t-girl will look, when printed with this resin.

What are the pros?

Have you watched their promo video on youtube, where they drill it, cut thread, machine the finished product?

Yes, that is all true. This resin has very different physical properties, compared to other resins. In fact, when cured, it does not feels like resin at all. In terms of tactile feeling, hardness, machinability and usability it sits somewhere in between of PVC, Teflon and hard modeling foam. All this allows making of such functional parts, which was not possible before with resin printing. Like tiny angle lever with M2 holes in it or replacement eyeglass hinge with M1.2 thread!

Also, it is "pitch black" - I mean, it is really black and not translucent, like some of other brands "black" resins.

But there is a HUGE disappointment - significant change of shape after curing or being exposed to normal daylight. Especially, when layer is thin. I did a following test, printed a plain stripe - 100mm length, 15 mm width, 2 mm thickness, using recommended settings, cured it and let it lay under normal indoor light for 3 days. It warped badly - almost formed 30 degree curve. For comparison, I printed same object using another brand (cheap) "ABS like" resin, which is very brittle and hard to machine, but it maintained its shape well. I altered both printing and curing times, to exclude errors - no luck, same warping for thin and long objects...

So conclusion is as follows: This resin has excellent machinability characteristics, but very bad dimensional stability, so I have no idea, where this can be used.

If you want both machineability and dimensional stability, I have a following "recipe", which works just fine on my AnyCubic M3. I'm using 60% of FlashForge "ABS-Like" resin, mixed with 40% of SuperFast's "SuperFlex" resin. I get good machineability and good dimensional stability.

Hope this helps...

Bottom line, a waste of my effort, time, and money.

Updated 10/08/2019:

The vendor lists this product as, "Electrically Conductive Epoxy, Silver Adhesive, Room Temperature Cure, Air Dry AA-DUCT 902 , 2.5gm kit". The key part here being, "Room Temperature Cure".

One week after application this product still had not cured and was the consistency of fresh window putty. From the other negative reviews on Amazon it was clear that I am not the only customer that had this problem. Several of them have mentioned needing to put the epoxy in an oven to get it to cure.

So I set my oven to 200 degrees and popped a couple of items with the never curing epoxy on them into the oven and went about doing home repairs. After three hours I removed them and set them aside to cool down.

I checked them once they had cooled and the epoxy had finally set. And the set epoxy was conductive as claimed.

But 200 degrees fahrenheit is in no way, shape, or form "ROOM TEMPERATURE", as advertised.

I will not mince words. This is FALSE AND MISLEADING ADVERTISING.

When you attempt to insert a lead, the tip of the lead will catch on the end of the internal spring clip, preventing the lead from slipping into the hole. It's frustrating to insert single leads at a time, and damned near impossible to insert multi-leaded devices, like headers and DIPs.

Buy better ones. I'm going to.

I’m refurbishing an older boat and that includes redoing a lot of the wiring. These switches provide an easy-to-use on/off rocker switch for everything from navigation lights to bilge pump to fishfinder.

These are made to install in a control panel or box, let’s say, that is up to 1/8-inch thick. Any more than that and the spring-clips on the sides won’t click in. One drawback in the USA: the mounting hole you need is 20mm diameter, not a common size in a drill-bit. Apart from buying one in metric size, you’ll need to finesse a hole about 25/32nds of an inch, about a millimeter wider than a ¾-inch bit. I did it by rotating the bit a little in the hole.

This PEI sheet fits on both my Ender 3 V2 and Ender 3 S1 perfectly. My machines already had a magnetic base applied so I can't speak to the effectiveness of the one in this kit. I recommend pulling up a YouTube video on applying the magnetic sheet to get the least amount of air bubbles trapped under it.

The tabs on the edge make it easy to lift the PEI sheet from the magnetic base. They also help with lining the PEI sheet up before starting a print.

The texture carries through to prints perfectly. You may want to run your nozzle a little lower than normal to force the plastic into the pits and valleys of the textured surface. I found that the Z offset that I use for my smooth PEI sheets was about 0.1mm too high.

I had no problems printing both PLA and PETG on this sheet. In general, PETG worked better for me, but that's what I primarily print so my machines are better tuned for it.

This sheet only has PEI on one side, that side being the textured one. The other side is exposed steel. You could put some painter's tape, Kapton tape, or hairspray on the steel side to get some adhesion, but I wouldn't recommend using it. If you're looking for PEI all around, there are some vendors here on Amazon selling dual-sided sheets where one side is textured PEI and the other is smooth PEI.

For the best adhesion, I recommend washing this sheet out of the box with some dish soap and warm water. Use the soft side of a sponge and gently work the soap into the textured PEI. I think sometimes these manufacturers put a light powder on the PEI, and it's best to wash that off before use. After washing, hit it with a few passes of isopropyl alcohol or Windex, then you're ready to go.

At the time of writing this review, the price of this PEI sheet was $16.99. That's a good price for what you're getting, and at the time seemed to be one of the cheapest options here on Amazon. It may be an introductory price to gain some market share or reviews, but that price is good nonetheless.

The UNI-T UT301A+ Infrared Thermometer is a compact unit that comes with the thermometer, required single 9V battery, carrying case, and a simple manual. Activating the unit is as simple as flipping the red grip section forward and inserting the 9V battery, then closing the grip. Pulling the trigger gives you a reading, although, like me, you'll likely want to switch from Celsius to Fahrenheit first.

Consistency is what matters most, even above pinpoint accuracy, which is difficult with a consumer infrared thermometer. Fortunately, the UNI-T has excellent consistency when reading temperatures from the same spot. I was able to get good readings from various air conditioning vents, behind TVs and game consoles, and other areas I wanted to check for hot or cold spots.

The thermometer's temperature range is -25.6 to 788 degrees Fahrenheit (-32 degrees to 420 degrees Celsius), with an average 250ms response time. There's also a high/low temperature reading and alarm, as well as lock measurements. The manual succinctly describes operating distance and effectiveness, as well as the emissivity (energy radiation) of various materials. In short, the UNI-T provides everything the non-professional would likely need in such a device. It's highly recommended.

First, make sure to remove the fuse for the AC unit, you don't want to get shocked.

Second, take a picture of the wiring to make sure to put back everything where it supposed to be.

Third, use a screwdriver with a plastic handle in order to short the current capacitor. Cross the C common with the Fan then do the same with the
Herm, that should do it. You don't want to die so do it a couple of times.

Fourth, use a niddle nose plier to remove the connectors, do not attempt to pull on the wire as they may break

Fifth, remove the old capacitor and set the new one instead.

Sixth, plug the wiring back, close the unit and re-plug the AC fuse.

Seventh, test your AC!

Fairly simple unless your unit is on the roof like mine where I have only 2 feet of clearance between the AC unit and a 25 feet drop. So if like me, use a harness to secure your fall in case gravity is calling you back!

Enjoy 5 to 8 years of cooling....!

I've been wanting a backpack vacuum for awhile and finally made the purchase after getting 2 cats, and I am very glad that I did.  This vacuum has powerful suction and lots of accessories that work very well, and having the backpack makes vacuuming around furniture and the gauntlet of cat toys easy.  The quality feels very durable to me, and I like that the telescoping wand is metal (not plastic) and very sturdy. I use the self-powered "turbo brush" floor tool to clean 1000 sq ft of hard floors (wood, pergo, and vinyl), 400 sq ft of berber carpeting, and two low-pile area rugs, and this vacuum does a fantastic job picking up everything including lots of cat hair and litter.  And the vacuum does pick up in both directions, I usually do push and pull over same area due to all the cat hair/litter, but I can see the vacuum picking up in both directions.  The width of the "turbo brush" floor tool is perfect for getting between and under furniture, and I no longer have to move any furniture when vacuuming - it's just small enough to fit everywhere and the "neck" that attaches to the wand turns 360 degrees so I can twist it sideways and get it under cabinets.  An unexpected bonus for me is that this vacuum does a GREAT job dusting my wood furniture when I use the small rectangular attachment (not the dusting brush tool) - it gets up all the cat hair (in addition to the dust) very quickly.  I also love that it has a stable base and a carry-handle on top so if I need to do a quick pick-up in one spot, I just carry it over rather that put on my back and it stays in place.  I was a little nervous about the weight, but I have not had any problems wearing it for the 45 mins I usually spend cleaning (I am a 5'4" woman and reasonably fit).  It does blow warm/hot air out the side, but I consider this a non-issue because it's no hotter than my previous upright vacuum and far easier and quicker to use.  To me, the only negative to this vacuum cleaner is that it makes vacuuming and dusting so easy that I have no excuse not to do them.

Works great. I was able to find the dimensions from a different product [[ASIN:B0771W9M6R [initeq] Threaded Heat Set Inserts for Plastics Combination (Imperial + Metric) Assortment A 200 Pack]]. I used .206 in. for the top hole and .185 in. for the bottom hole, with a distance of .250 in. I also extended the .185 in. hole to the length of my screw. For the screw, I used [[ASIN:B000CZ4HFM The Hillman Group 101040 6-32-Inch x 1-1/2-Inch Flat Head Phillips Machine Screw, 100-Pack]].

I performed a stress test on this after setting it in a test block. I tried tweaking the screw sideways to see if the nut would come loose, but the screw bent. I then attempted to hammer on the screw from the back side (bottom side) of the nut test whether the nut would pop out. The screw bent, but the nut didn't budge. As a final test, I used a wrench to tighten the screw as far as I could. I expected the threads of the nut, being brass, would strip out or the nut would start spinning in the plastic. But... the head of the screw broke. :P I removed the remnants of the screw, and while there was slight damage to the threads, the nut still worked with a new screw without problem.

I was a little surprised I was not able to get the nut to even budge in the block. I printed with PLA, 5 layer outlines. I think this certainly helped to retain the nut. To insert the nut, I used my Weller WESD51 set to the lowest heat setting, which is 350 F. I didn't force the nuts in, but allowed the weight of the soldering iron to work the nut into position.

The only way these nuts are coming out of the PLA block is with heat. I'm pleasantly impressed with these, and this should allow me to expand the types of projects I can create with my 3D printer.

While this might seem pricier compared to glue sticks or hairspray its well worth the cost. Glue sticks worked so so for me. Hairspray worked but then left residue on the bottom to clean up. Also with hairspray you had to be careful not to overspray. With Magigoo you apply right on the area you want. You don't need to prep the whole bed unless you need to for a huge print. While the bottle says to apply new material to the bed each print, but I could get a lot more per application. But to be 100%, I would follow their instructions. Once the bed cools down you just simply take the part off by hand. The applicator tip ripped off and they sent me two replacements free of charge. I've printed with PLA, ASA, ABS, PETG with success with Magigoo. While you might get away with a cold bed for PLA, I've always had better luck with a heated bed and adhesive. I plan on getting their PC version shortly to print with Polycarbonate.

Oh ya some additional stuff: glue sticks also left residue to clean up. hair spray smell yuck. The number of prints varied if same model printed over and over in same spot. But I've gotten 5-20 per an application reducing cost per print a lot. To prep for use I clean off bed with hot water and dry. I spread on Magigoo where I need it and the material dries quickly.

These spools claim a consistent diameter of 1.75 give or take 0.05. Most spools I buy claim the same however I have not once actually /seen/ this amount of variance when measuring the diameter. Most spools seem to measure lows and highs of 1.73 - 1.76. Within a one foot stretch of this filament I can see 1.70 to 1.8mm depending on where I measure. That is within the product's described tolerance so I cannot fault it for that. But I cannot wonder if it is the cause of the slight variance in printed layers that is visible when under direct light. Printed 210/72 Prusa MK3S with full Bear Upgrade, textured PEI sheet. Pictures are after some basic extrusion multiplier adjustment and LA calibration @ .2mm layer height.

Like any filament purchase there are far too many variables to judge quality off of the finished print. Not to mention differences in color and batch. I have had small difficulties with adhesion but again that could just be me. I have not yet tried the black roll that I ordered.

Be ready for bruised hands if doing many of these without the proper crimper, but still these are perfect. Does exactly what you want for 4 Gauge wires. I crimped them with Vise-Grips, and with some technique they crimped nicely!

Vise-Grip procedure:
Insert twisted 4GA wire, and get all the little wires into the connector all at once using a careful twisting motion, should be plenty of space. Crimp slowly until the middle split starts to fold in. Individually crimp each side more, until looking inside the connector the metal goes from a "D" shape to a "B" shape, splitting the cable mostly in half to either side of the "B".

IMPORTANT: If connector is not in a "B" shape but looks like "6" or "9" you have messed up. Straighten out connector and try again. Otherwise the connection may pull free! This is not a product defect, but a technique error, work on it!

Some small wires will come out of the middle of the "B" while crimping, and that's ok. The black or red cable jacket will cover any errant little wires from the cable. There should only be a few. If many come out you have messed up with a "6" or "9". Straighten out the connector and try again.

If all is well and you have a nice "B" shape, I'd use another bigger pair of Vise-Grips to close the "B" into more of a "=", meaning I'd crimp the connector sideways to close off the "B", with emphasis on crimping the cable base here more than the ring side. This creates friction that guarantees a solid crimp.

Afterwards be sure to pull on the newly crimped connector, not with full strength but enough to ensure that daily usage will not disrupt the connection!

Good luck, and happy crimping. This is what you want for 4GA connectors, they are the best on Amazon, also buy these for the big 3. You won't regret it.x

I've gone through probably a half-dozen different kinds of organizers looking for a good way to keep track of small circuitry components. This is hands down the best one I've used for surface-mount components.

Sewing organizers and tackle boxes are better for larger parts, like things larger than your fingernail, but this is great for smaller stuff. The smallest parts I use are 0603, but I don't have trouble with anything falling out. The drawers also stay shut very well.

There aren't many cons, but the labels aren't very easy to write on. I just use a label printer to print part names out in a small font. The drawers are small, but I think it's a good compromise with how many there are. They're about 15mm wide and seem to fit about a thousand 0805 resistors comfortably. They're just large enough for a 0.5mm-pitch QFP100 chip to lie flat in, although you should probably use the pricier anti-static version of this box for things that require ESD protection.

Anyways, it's also small enough to put in a bag and carry around, which is very nice considering how many parts you can fit in it.

My old multimeter was from a big box tool store. It was a constant frustration. The leads were too short and needed frequent repair where they connected to the probe tips. It was time for a replacement.

Wow, I was pleasantly surprised when I received this meter. First off, the leads are plenty long for my uses, nearly twice the length of those of my old meter. The lead ends have strain relief and silicone shielding. Both are good features for longevity. The meter itself is solid and has a good feel in hand. The display is easy to read and is backlit.

The available tests are organized a bit differently than I’m used to, but nothing major. Several test types are combined under one dial setting, the test desired can be changed within each dial position by pressing the SEL (select) button. The test type displays on the meter screen and in the app, if connected. This meter displays temperature from the included probe in Fahrenheit or Celsius. I’ve not had a multimeter that displayed temperatures before and am looking forward to using it for various projects.

Having the app, enables easy reading and recording of values and even the ability to read the meter from a distance. The only limitation to reading via the app is to be within Bluetooth range. The app shows values on an analog dial, which is handy to quickly see changes in readings.

As others have mentioned, the battery cover requires a very small Phillips screwdriver, size 00. I did not have any issues installing the included 9V battery.

The package includes the meter, a pair of test leads, a temperature probe with coiled wire, a case, 9V battery and instruction book. (See pic)

I’m very happy with this new multimeter. My old meter is going out the door and I hope this review has been helpful.

These copper connectors are SC35-10 and are very solidly built. The set gives you 10 of the most common used lugs. It does not come with a crimping tool, but it does give you the heat shrink tubes which is an added bonus. I have a couple of different size crimping tools so this was not a big deal for me, but someone who doesn't have one may want to know it doesn't have one.
This set is not exhaustive, but it is very good set to have when you need it from time to time. Various size lugs will fit most applications, but there might be times when you'll have to go to the hardware store to find that specific size that you need. This is the new and improved set that you get, where quality standards and thickness have been increased.
The copper is high temperature resistant, as well as anti corrosion proof. They are commercial grade and very durable. A must-have for any DIYer, the lugs are 100% pure copper, and when fastened correctly, your wire will not slip out.
Only one criticism, the thickness of the terminals do not increase as the size goes up. For the smaller size lugs the thickness is more than enough. For the medium size lugs the thickness is perfect, but for the larger size lugs 2mm more would have been better. Yet, they did increase the thickness with this latest revision. Great value and I highly recommend it.

Regarding both DACS and amps, the law of diminishing returns starts at around $350 for the pair. The purpose of this pair is to take a digital signal from a computer device and make it into an analog signal that is sufficiently loud. Solid state amps do the best job at that, as they do not color, distort, mute, and add noises (popping, hissing, etc.) like tube amps do. As such, a $350 portable JDS Labs O2 amp and Standalone ODAC pairing will achieve 95% of the audio quality of any $5,000 or even $50,000 setup, marketing spam notwithstanding. A great alternative pairing is the $199 Schiit Magni 2 and Modi 2, but they are not portable and you may have to upgrade to the costlier Uber models of both (another $120 or so) to achieve compatibility with your equipment. Empirical evidence is minimal in the audio industry, which has opened the doors for outlandish manufacturers' claims that rationalize the ridiculously inflated prices of their products. Third-party measurements of sensitivity, efficiency, and the like are some of the few characteristics that can be objectively measured. Proud to support the American Worker. I replaced my condenser fan motor and capacitor four years ago on my 17 year old Trane. The old cap was still in specs but for very little money for a USA made capacitor it was a no brainer. I've used Genteq's in the past with no problems but their made in Mexico. I do like that Amrad warranties them for their licensed contractors customers for 5 years, that says a lot about their parts and quality control. I know it doesn't apply to me as a DIY but I'm ok with that. Two years ago Morris Jenkins replaced my neighbors HVAC system for $13,000. The first day it hit 96 degrees this summer their AC wouldn't work. They had no AC for hours by the time the tech came out to figure out the problem under warranty. It was the dual run capacitor and even he said they used cheap capacitors. I'd be ticked to find out I spent that much to have a cheap capacitor used and only last two summer seasons. Leaving my family in the heat on the first hot day of the next summer, ridiculous.

For DIY out there take care in replacing these. It's easy but can be dangerous make sure to watch videos on how to. Get a multimeter and pull the disconnect or shut the power off anytime you go to replaced one of these. Always re check for power at the contactor terminals plus remember to discharge the old capacitor. Next I will order a 10mf Amrad cap to replace my blower motor cap inside the house. It about four years old too but still in spec. Again, cheap quality replacements when you don't want the old ones to dump out when it's a hundred degrees outside where I live in South Carolina.

I've been buying this brand exclusively for many years now for pro AV work. There are a lot of tapes out there claiming to be "gaffer" tape that are nothing more than duct/duck tape with a matt finish. Most of them leave adhesive behind and some aren't even cloth backed. This is the real deal- it blocks light, has a matt black (if black is ordered) finish, and the adhesive, while strong, releases cleanly. Yes- it's more expensive- because it is the real thing. I have yet to have a cable, stand, carpet, wall, backdrop, mic, camera, speaker, or anything else ruined by this tape. I can't say that for cheaper alternatives I've tried.

I feel compelled to address some of the bad reviews I've seen:
Gaffer tape is gaffer tape! It is not duct/duck tape, and while it can do a lot more- it is designed to -temporarily- affix and mark items for stage and screen, photography, videography, lighting, AV, etc. It is not permanent, it isn't an automotive or construction adhesive, it isn't electrical tape, etc. If you leave any tape for months or years, or out in the sun- it is going to leave adhesive and probably damage something, or it is just going to come undone. If you aren't using it for its purpose- it will disappoint. That's not the fault of Pro Tape, or any real gaffer tape manufacturer.

My husband HATES to sweep and mop & what woman doesn't need her husband's help with housework? When our anniversary came around, I was looking for something he would "use" and something that would also be useful for me. So I got the Neato XV-21. This vacuum saves him so much time (and my sanity) it's unbelievable! The main level in our home is approximately 3100 sq ft. We have hardwood, tile, area rugs,and carpet. "She" will methodically work "her" way around the house and as "her" battery runs low "she" will work "her" way slowly back to the base to re-charge. Once the re-charging is complete "she" takes off again remembering where "she" left off. If I only need "her" to clean the common areas of the home (about 2100 sq ft) it will usually complete that with 2 charges(the starting one & one re-charge) unless we forget and leave "obstacles" on the floor, causing Neato to have to navigate more. If I have "her" clean the entire 3100 sq ft it'll take at least 3 charges. The only situations we've run in to that I would warn about are bar stools and a 1970's circular breakfast table, my husband & I turned into a pub table. The bar stool bases are just wide enough that "she" can go between the legs at an angle but can't get out. I put the bar stools upside down on the breakfast bar - problem solved. The pub table has one center post that goes all the way to the floor and 4 flat legs coming out from that base for the stabilization. Those legs are about 1 inch high at the highest point but "she" gets stuck on them. I put the barrier around it - another problem solved. The only downsides are (1)the kids leaving obstacles on the floor and no one is home to help "her" get them unstuck from her brush and (2)If I'm not going to have the time or don't want to sweep in the near future, I sweep around the walls, corners, and under the couch moving it all toward the middle of the floor so "she" can get all the dirt/dust("she" doesn't get neat to the walls very well). Also, not a downside, I noticed that the filter gets dusty very quickly even if you clean the dust bin often. I put in my extra one(I ordered extras) and put the dusty one in the dishwasher(as suggested by another reviewer)and it comes out as good as new. Just let it dry completely before using it again. I promise this, "she" has helped solved my frustrating issue of him not helping with housework when I have a full-time job and we have 3 kids, 2 of which play sports.

I purchased the Qidi Tech X-Max 3d printer in August of 2019 and have had it for almost 11 months at the time of writing this review. I am not an expert in 3d printing nor claim to know what is best, this is just a review of my experience. It was my first 3D printer and did a lot of research. I was looking for something that was large format, quiet, versatile, well made, and little hassle. I read many reviews, specs, and forums along with several video reviews and how tos. It was far from the cheapest model I could have selected but I was not looking for cheap.
Packaging:
When I received the printer it was very well packed and secured in the box with ample Styrofoam around and in it. It came with 2 full 1kg rolls of filament (1 PLA and 1 ABS), tool kit, instructions, 2 removal magnetic build plates, and 2 extruders (1 high temp, and 1 normal).
Construction:
The external encloser is a nice durable ABS plastic with clear front door and clear dome top. The inside is strong metal framing and has clean routing of the wires. It is not small and is a bit heavy but feels well made.
Performance:
It took me less than 20 min from unboxing to starting my first print off of the supplied USB stick. Most of that time was the unboxing. As far as slicing software, I use the supplied Qidi Print slicer which works well for what I am using it for. Many others use Cura or S3D which is fine, but I have had no issues with Qidi Print. Leveling the bed is key so take your time and triple check it with a bed level print in between and it will save a lot of time. I rarely have to relevel the bed, usually if I change out the extruder. Since I have purchased this printer, I have purchased other cheaper popular printers and the X-Max has me spoiled. The X-max is incredibly quiet with the top cover on it and the door closed. It has had no problem doing prints ranging form .08 to .2 layer height and has creats very detailed prints. It has an Ethernet port, USB port, and Wifi. The Ethernet and USB ports are in the front which in my option is not the greatest spot. I use wifi so the ethernet port is not a big deal and I use a very stubby USB stick which took care of the concern of the USB drive sticking out to far. Wifi Connectivity works well but can be slow sending the print jobs to the printer if the files are large. I am ok with this since I am not a fan of jockeying pen drives back and forth.
Service and support:
The service, support, and Warranty from Qidi Tech is something I have never seen from any vendor on any product. On the minor issues I have had I have received an email in less then 24 hours with the answer to my question. If any part is needing replaced there is no hassle and I have received the part in just a few days with detailed instructions or videos on how to address the issue. They even went the extra mile helping with settings on a very detailed print that I was having trouble with. They went as far as taking the STL I was trying to print and running it through one of their inhouse X-Max printers and sending me the settings that best worked. This type of customer service is amazing.
Cons:
The spool holder is not the best design but works well enough. There are plenty of modifications that people have created on Thingiverse to address this. The internal spool holder for high temp materials is a good concept but is cumbersome and the filament routing is awkward but again works and is functional. I don’t use high temp filament so not an issue for me. It does have a resume feature when power is lost but there is not Filament runout sensor. Many seasoned printing enthusiasts don’t care about this but I think it would be a nice to have.
Summary:
Over all I am very happy with the X-max printer! It is a work horse, Well made, and runs darn near 24x7 for me. The Customer service is amazing and very helpful. If you are looking for a solid printer that is easy to use I would recommend the X-Max

[[VIDEOID:a23270ca4b27baef82eda4badf718e]] Wow this thing puts out some serious heat! I converted a Liquid Propane turkey fryer to natural gas for ease of use and eliminating the need to get propane refills. This burner got my 34 Qt pot boiling in less than 15 minutes. Seafood boils are now a breeze!

See pictures and video for details. If this review helped you let me know by marking as helpful thanks!

(Disclaimer -Use at own risk / for informational purposes only / follow all local code rules and regulations)

These are the parts I used to convert:
- Bayou Classic High Pressure 14 inch Cooker Model # SP10 ASIN# B000291GBQ
- 1/2 inch by 10 inch black gas pipe - Orange Big Box store SKU #1001790506
- Midline Gas Ball Valve - Model # GUHW-5IS34G ASIN# B00OQA75W6
- Harvey Gas PTFE thread seal tape - ASIN# B000FKBXCE
- 2 Stainless steel hose clamps - check your garage you probably have these laying around lol

How to:
- The Bayou Classic burner is held on by 1 screw on the bottom, unscrew it and remove the burner.
- I bent the original mounting bracket down to an L shape an inch or two lower than original to have the burner sit as close to level as possible without having to cut up the stand housing.
- Use the 2 SS hose clamps to secure the jet burner to the mounting bracket.
- The 1/2 inch black pipe can now thread into the burner - make sure to use Yellow sealant tape or pipe dope rated for gas.
- Install the Gas Ball Valve on the other end of the 1/2 inch pipe.
- My outdoor Weber natural gas grill line uses a 3/8 flare female connection which connects perfectly to the other side of the Ball gas valve.
- To light just open the ball valve less than a quarter turn and use a long neck lighter
- Once a burner is lit, you can slowly turn the gas higher so that the rest of the burners will light.

I applied this product over 3 month old, Mannington Luxury Sheet Vinyl.. When we installed the expensive, new vinyl, the surface was disappointingly course. It felt like sandpaper under my bare feet. The application was done over two days in a bathroom and kitchen. I began by scrubbing the floor with ammonia and water and a scrub brush. After thoroughly rinsing and drying, I applied 2 coats of Zep commercial sealer. Next, I applied 4 coats of the Zep Wet Look Floor Finish Gloss. I was careful to allow a minimum of 30 minutes drying time between coats. This was done over 2 days. The second day it rained and it took 1 hour in between coats for the floor to feel dry enough for the next coat. Spills dry quickly and are hard to remove, so I had to be careful to keep a rag with me and wipe up any spills immediately. All applications were done on my hands and knees with cotton rags from old t-shirts. I found that pouring the product directly onto the floor worked better than putting it in a bucket.

I have been a ARIZONA registered master heat pump technician for over 25 years.
The problem I have noticed with capacitors is that many of them are defective out of the box.
The reason I say that is I test the microfarads while the capacitor is under load which will tell me it’s exact microfarad rating. This is done by checking the amps and volts wile it is running. I use what I call the 2652 method.
The simple formula is Start Winding Amps X 2,652 ÷ Capacitor Voltage = Microfarads.
Sample: 5 amps Times 2652 divided 369 volts =35µF

This is the correct way to test a capacitor. There are meters that have capacitor testers settings on them but I never used them because they are pretty much useless unless you just wanna know what size it is. You need to put a capacitor under load to make sure it doesn’t have any leaking Through that dielectric.
This capacitor I have bought several times and it is exact to what it is rated at.
Some brands of air conditioners you will find bad capacors on every one of them when you fire them up new. I don’t wanna mention any names but one that does this the most makes air conditioners that start with the letter C and another brand with the letter B. They actually buy rejected capacitors for their units to get them cheaper so sad.
It’s very important to have a correctly size capacitor to create a third leg properly. This is basically making a third phase. If you’re capacitor is leaking electricity through the dielectric it will shorten the life of your unit. About 25% of brand new air conditioner run capacitors do not pass the test.
They can only be as far as 10% off of what they’re rated at is there any greater than that it’s best to throw them away. It’s also a good thing to change your air conditioning run capacitor at least every four years. In hotter states possibly more often.
They make a 370 V and the 440 V capacitors
I highly recommend going with the 440 V rating it will put up with more heat and will last longer.
The 440 V rating only means how much electricity it can handle. So it’s basically heavier duty than the 380V ones. Your air conditioner might be 220 V but when the compressor is running the voltage across the run cap can double that. So be warned if you’re going to test a live Ron cab you’re going to have to be extremely careful because the voltage coming off that run cap can kill you.
With that being said I recommend this brand.

Second, I purchased this to completely wire a new horn on my old truck from scratch (momentary button, this relay, inline fuse, horns, wiring - the works), and when I first did my test wire-up, it did not work (not this relay specifically, but my wire-up based on a lot of different diagrams out on the web).  Fortunately, the horns I purchased (duals from Harbor Freight for $10) had the correct wiring schematic [side note: + on the battery to an inline fuse to relay PIN30 (which gets wire-connected to relay PIN86 also); relay PIN85 to momentary switch; relay PIN87 to horns; relay PIN87a in the center unused].  All these PIN refs are clearly marked on the relay, which makes matching the colored wires on the socket easy.  [Side note2 to serious DIYselfers: you really only need the relay (or not - the horns I noted above included a relay), and not the socket (you would put your own female connectors on your own wires), but this included socket made the temporary wiring and testing much faster and easier. This printer is actually my 2nd printer. I had a 3d printer a few years ago in roughly the same price point from monoprice and had a lot of trouble dialing it in, only getting a few successful prints and then storing it away. This printer has been a breeze in comparison, pretty much out of the box there is very little needed for setup. There was a 3d printed cover over a metal piece I had to remove which was not mentioned in any guide, after that just using the application provided on the sd card and leaving things on default I was able to print things straight from thingiverse, playing around with speed, supports, and rafts. You do quickly come into some limitations of this printer and I'll list them below.

Cons:
1. Bed size: very small bed, often have to orient 3d objects in certain ways or shrink them in order to print. Still very useable but very quickly you'll design or come across something wide or long that won't fit.
2. Does not support PETG or ABS: This means you are limited to using PLA filament which is good for display things but not so much functional. PLA melts easily and has weak vertical bonds. I found this out quickly when I tried to make a glasses holder for the car and it went soft and melted in a day because it was printed in PLA.
3. The arm that holds filament is very short so you can only fit small spools of filament. On thingiverse you can find an extended arm you can print which is a workaround but I feel like it makes the filament come at an odd angle. It's easier to use small spools due to this limitation.

Lastly I wish this had a preheat function, sometimes the first print comes out a little wonky.

Despite these cons I still give this printer 5 stars because it is so easy to use, affordable, and fun and as long as you're aware of these limitations and you're looking for your first printer I think this is a great choice.

Works great...once you know how to use it properly. I used this for adding a clear coat of epoxy for tumblers. I was a total beginner when I started and learned a few things along the way that might help people like me:
1) put both bottles in the sink and fill it with warm water. Let sit for about 10 minutes. I learned the hard way that if the resin is too cold it won’t mix with the hardener properly and the result is a sticky mess. After numerous you tube videos, I found this tip and it worked great! Warming it up also helps get rid of most of the bubbles.
2) The 1:1 ratio is critical. I accidentally added a bit more hardener once(because it pours faster) and didn’t think it would make much of a difference. It does. The result never lost the tacky feel.
3) Mix for at least a minute or two. It feels like forever as your mixing, but I found the longer I mixed, the more consistent my results turned out as I mixed resin for fifteen cups in the span of two weeks. I ruined a couple cups by not mixing it enough. The results were sticky no matter how long it dried.
4) If you’re making tumblers, a “cuptisserie” motorized cup Turner is a MUST. The resin is very fluid and does not like to stay in place. Applying the resin as it’s turning was the only way possible.

I used the app from the HDMI organization to verify that the cable was certified as stated and it came back with the same information shown in the product photos. This is a legitimate certification, proving that this specific model and length of cable underwent testing to not only show that it works, but also that it did not emit harmful RF interference which could affect things like WiFi, cellular, Bluetooth, etc.

The cable is currently connecting my HD TV to my Denon A/V receiver and it's working flawlessly. It is replacing an older cable that isn't up to the current HDMI 2.1 standard. Whether using this cable will result in any functional, audible, or visible improvements seems doubtful -- until I upgrade the TV.

Bottom line: When a certified HDMI 2.1 cable is available at this price, it makes no sense to buy one that is not certified. If, using a certified cable, you encounter some problem, the seller of your TV, streaming device, DVR, A/V receiver, etc. can't get away with blaming the cable.

Most important thing. MAKE SURE THE POWER SUPPLY IS SET TO THE RIGHT VOLTAGE. If you don't know what that means, don't buy this printer. If assembling IKEA furniture intimidates you, or you are uncomfortable with working from rudimentary instructions that don't provide much detail, don't but this printer. I have worked in technical assembly/design for over 20 years, and had zero problems; but I can easily see how someone that doesn't have the same sort of experiences could struggle, especially if they aren't into troubleshooting in the event that they happen to flub a step. Not that you will need them (they are included), but if you don't own a set of hex wrenches, this printer probably isn't for you.

I set this up with my 15 year old son. If he was doing it by himself, I'm not sure it would have been put together properly; at least not on the first try. However, he was able to operate it on his own after only a few days of tutelage.

I see lots of complaints about warped beds. That hasn't been my experience. If my bed IS warped, it's so minimal that it isn't effecting my prints (I use a raft for all my prints, which may help with that). I'm also seeing a lot of complaints about bed leveling. Again, not my experience. Bed leveling isn't difficult, but it can be time consuming to get right, so be patient and seek advice on the inter-webs. If you're unsure, DON'T TRY TO GUESS YOUR WAY THROUGH THE PROCESS. I've had an less headaches leveling this printer that I ever had with my auto-leveling Monoprice Delta printer. Some of the leveling complaints I'm reading lead me to believe that some people didn't setup the z-axis switch at the right height; so make doubly sure you have it set how the instructions state.

As for print quality; I don't know what one would expect from a printer at this price point, but I'm happy with the quality for what I paid.

I wouldn't recommend this printer for anyone with zero experience with 3D printing, zero experience with this sort of machinery, or who just isn't into assembling their own stuff. However, if you ARE a complete noob to printing, BUT have experience with similar equipment and software, or have 3d printing experience/knowledge, like building stuff, but have never owned a printer; I would give this a recommendation.

[UPDATE on 1/1/23: our total electricity consumption in 2022 dropped even further to just 5,500 kWh (1,600 of which was for HVAC) for the year. We have HALVED our electricity consumption. Huge savings. This thermal imager continues to operate beautifully. We lend it to friends & family so they can do their own diagnostics to save energy.]

We first used our Klein Tools TI250 Rechargeable Thermal Imager to identify where our home’s protective envelop was weak – places where we were losing heat / allowing cold air inside in the winter and losing cool air / allowing heat inside in the summer. The imager revealed problem areas we had suspected, e.g., around windows and doors – areas where we needed to improve weatherstripping. But above all they highlighted an extremely acute problem we hadn’t focused on, namely the 7 recessed lights in our kitchen. In summer, and with those lights off, the thermal imager showed the lights as 7 ultra-bright, fiercely orange circles, though the ceiling all around (under thick insulation) was deep, cool blue. I have been using this thread sealer for over 22 years and have assembled 10's of thousands of NPT threaded joints with it. Rarely will I get a leak. I have used this alone and also with PTFE tape. The reason for the tape and the sealer used together is that most of my NPT joints are plastic Polypropylene/PVC/CPVC and Kynar. Sometimes plastic NPT joints/threads can be a little sloppy from manufacturer to manufacturer so using both in this scenario fills in the larger gaps and creates a leak free joint pretty much every time.  In my experience it will NOT harden rock hard but will set up and remain pliable pretty much indefinitely . Once set up you can touch it and it will not want to stick back on you. This thread sealer does not have the little bits of PTFE in it like some of the other brands of thread sealer.  The color of this stuff is a bluish green and it has an exceptionally smooth thick consistency. If properly applied it will not run.  If you let it sit in the can for extended periods you will need to mix it with the included in-can brush before use. If I get it on my skin I use a strong alcohol like isopropyl or others to clean it off. The only annoyance I find with it is the rubber seal in the cap sometimes sticks to the rim of the can and comes out of the cap upon opening. I remedy this by putting a little bit of adhesive in between the inside of the metal cap and then put the rubber seal back in. I have tried other thread sealers but this is my go to product. Excellent! Hope it helps. Cheers!

I got perplexed installing a water hammer arrestor. The water hammer arrestor was labeled "1/4" O.D." But its male fittings were 1/4" inside diameter (I.D.). I couldn't understand why this 1/4" I.D. female coupler slid over the male fittings. The male fittings were 0.43" and this female couple is 0.455". After spending way too much time searching on the Internet I put on my mask and went to Home Depot. The plumbing aisle employee told me that the water hammer arrestor had a compression fitting. I went home and found a YouTube video explaining how to connect compression fittings. Twenty minutes later I'd installed my water hammer arrestor, with no extra parts. So I never used this brass coupler but it looks nice. :-)

My pipe is 0.25" inside diameter and the outside diameter of the male threads are 0.43". This coupling has an inside diameter of the female threads of 0.44". Okay, so I used this to attach 2 Ikea carpets together to make a bigger one! Once you unwrap the tape,
1: attach to back side of carpet (make sure it is aligned)
2: use a rag that is wet, (not soaked but wet) and place it over the brown part of the tape.

THE YELLOW SIDE SHOULD BE FACING AND TOUCHING THE CARPET

3: use a iron, any kind will do as long as you lower the setting I used heat 4 from a standard Walmart iron. And going ON TOP of the rag go over it multiple times, about 30-40 seconds to make sure it melts together!

Important note: I found that using moisture on a rag is best, it was quicker and did not smell like burning tire when used.

4: once the entire section you want is dried you can take off the paper surrounding the yellow. You can leave it on I found out that it did not effect the durability of the adhesive!

I'm running a direct drive mod on my Ender 3 and a BMG dual gear clone. With this setup, I cut a 3mm piece of bowden tube to put inside the extruder to snug it up against the hotend and mounted this hotend directly into the BMG extruder. Filament changes are easy, the screw in thermistor is a game changer (especially since it comes with a connector and extension, so next time I need to change it I don't have to pull it all the way out of the mainboard... Though, since it's not a flimsy piece of glass, will I need to change it as often anyway?)

Honestly it's been printing like a dream with PLA so far (I am replacing a Microswiss hotend that I managed to bend several degrees out of square when I was moving).

Current PLA direct drive settings:
Hotend: 192C
Bed: 60C
Retraction: 1.2mm@20mm/s
Nozzle: 0.4mm (though I tend to prefer 0.5 or 0.6 -- I'm keeping the stock nozzle on this for now out of convenience)

Printer: Ender 3
Printer Firmware: Klipper (with a Raspberry Pi 2B running Klipper/Fluidd)
Bed: Creality glass bed (smooth side up)
Direct drive mount: Printermods MDD 1.3
Extruder: BMG clone

UPDATE: My heat break broke while I was tightening everything down to stop a leaking nozzle. GCR sent me a replacement right away. Great customer service.

I had been looking at 3 D printers for a while and when I spotted one that looked promising and even if it had been given a four star rating, reading the reviews made me skeptical. This one had eleven five star reviews when I decided to take the plunge, and here is one more. I had no prior experience with 3 D printing, I understood the process but never saw one in real life operation, this little machine makes learning easy. The machine is very easy to use once you have it set up, although I did find a couple of things I did not like about the design.
First the Z axis drive was too close to the column, the lead screw was not parallel to the column. The machine worked but this condition put some strain on the stepper when the gantry was in the lowest position, I added a .032" brass shim between the motor mount and the column and this almost brought the two parts parallel for the length of the screw.
Second, the bracket that mounts the guide wheel and lead screw nut to the gantry can not be adjusted one the machine is assembled. I was unable to level the table initially because gantry was out of square with the columns, I could square up the gantry but there was no way to tighten the screws to try to hold it in that position. I used a machinist square to get the gantry aligned with column on the drive side and then drilled two 1/8" holes through the gantry and wheel mount and used SS dowels to secure the alignment of the two pieces.
Lastly, even after resolving the gantry problem the spring on one corner of the bed was not very compressed compared to the other springs after leveling the bed, so I added a couple of washers under the spring, seems to have done the trick.
It took four tries to get the sample doggy printed using Hatchbox PLA, first one warped after about 1/8" of buildup using the programed bed and nozzle temps, lowered them both. Second and third wouldn't stick to the bed, too much clearance between the nozzle and bed, forth time was the charm with nozzle at 195 C and the bed at 35 C.
I am using Cura for my slicer and have a old version of Solid Works that I have used for 3 D modeling. I am going to try Tinkercad next.
Despite the problems I encountered, for the price and ease of use I still feel the machine deserves *****

Tourniquets are an item you have with you and hope that you never have to use them. So this review is based on my experience in the field, rather that having used this item in a real emergency.

I would rate these as a pretty good tourniquet. I know that comfort is not the goal of a tourniquet, but these were not all that uncomfortable. The windlass tightened up quickly and was able to cut off the pulse in my leg adequately. The hardware is strong enough that I did not feel like anything would break when the pressure was applied. The securing strap for the windlass is also white and able to be written on to write a time when the tourniquet was placed. The windlass did not create any unnecessary pinch points that would cause undue damage or discomfort. Overall these are pretty good tourniquets.

The one thing that I did not like was the packaging. They come in a sealed plastic bag with instructions. So the only way I can inspect the item for defects before placing it in service is to remove it from the bag. Then, to keep the tourniquet and the instructions together, I have to place them in another resealable bag. This one simple thing would make a world of difference in being able to use these more effectively in the field.
These tourniquets will be placed in my medical bag for Search and Rescue.

I am using the temp stick in a cabin located on a mountain where it gets very very cold. I did a lot of research comparing remote temperature monitors before buying Temp Stick. I ran the Temp Stick all summer and fall to determine its reliability and alert capability. The sensor is spot on, same read out as the temperature on the thermostat.

I've ordered a second Temp Stick; in addition, I am using lithium batteries. Call it overkill, but I want to know if the temperature in the cabin begins to drop! I don't want/need a repeat of last winter.

Initially, I had a few questions setting up the temp stick. My questions were answered promptly, professionally, and thoroughly by tech support. I called again recently; Josh in tech support demonstrated just how important customer service is with this company.

Temp Stick is providing the peace of mind I need in anticipation of another very cold, freezing winter.
