I got these casters to replace a set I had on my custom built kayak stand. It holds two full size 13 foot kayaks with loads of fishing gear. The old wheels were too small. They wouldn't swivel easy, so it was hard to move around. They also wouldn't go over the bump in the concrete to go in and out of my garage.

Enter these wheels. They're similar load capacity, but larger diameter than what I had. I was pleasantly surprised that I was able to remove the old casters, and bolt these right on. The mounting plate seems fairly universal, so it should work in most applications where you're replacing another set of wheels.

These wheels have a hard poly/rubber type material. I'm not dragging the thing down the road behind my truck, but going in and out of the garage, they're taking no wear at all. My kayak cart is probably 3-400lbs or so with the kayaks on board, but it's big and awkward with two big kayaks on it. Never mind all the junk piled on the kayaks, you'll see the cart in the pictures.

The garage has about a 3/4" lip where the driveway is lower, and pushing the cart in with the old wheels was impossible. You had to lift the cart up over the bump. These wheels roll right over it like it's not even there. I was bracing to ram full speed ahead over that hump, and it slid by like it was nothing. My back is happy about that.

The lock on these wheels is FIRM. It's a solid thunk when it locks in, and takes a good tug to pop up. It's not difficult, it's just sturdy and reliable. The cart won't roll if even just one wheel is locked.

I can push the kayak cart sideway with ease, despite whatever direction the wheels are facing. This used to be a major pain in the back trying it with the old wheels. These allow 100% freedom of movement. It just glides wherever I want it.

Finally price. The price of these things is great. Some wheels can be this much for ONE wheel! I wouldn't hesitate to recommend these. These are smooth rolling, strong locking sturdy well made wheels. I would definitely recommend them and wouldn't hesitate to acquire another set in the future.

People who are giving this product a one star provide reasons that are misleading. I have purchased 4 of these units, and I have compared them all next to $5,000+ professional Radon testing equipment. I have a unique perspective because my brother is a home inspector in Southwest Colorado. You should NEVER compare readings from this unit to other consumer-available testing equipment to reach a “reviewable” conclusion for the Amazon community.

If you purchase this product and think the reading are askew then start calling Radon remediation companies in your area. I have yet to find a region of the United States where I have been turned down by a remediation company for a free 24-72 hour test in which you can test this device’s readings. They all want the business if your results are high…

I am not saying this company may send a bad apple or two that was calibrated improperly but the four I purchased had no such issue. I imagine if you receive one with questionable results and provide a professional’s test along with the RD200’s results, and they are completely different, Amazon or the seller would replace the device.

I have tested Airthings, charcoal kits, other digital consumer measurement devices and NOTHING comes close to the accuracy of this unit.

Again, I have no interest or receive no benefit by submitting this review, but people should not put their health at risk by buying a subpar consumer measurement device due to the absurd one star reviewers.

I used window-weld about 2.5 months ago to repair the rear glass on my wife 2006 Audi A4 Cabrio. I also ordered the primer that is suggested to use with the window weld. In my haste, I forgot to apply the primer before the window-weld and the bond still took very well and seems to be holding up nicely.

First, I cleaned the area thay the windoweld would be applied to. Scraping off all old adhesive and cleaning with alcohol.

Second, I taped off areas that i did not want the window-weld to touch (I used painters tape-see pics).

Third, I applied the window-weld and clamps with the assistance of interior pressure (accomplished via rolled up towels) to be sure that solid pressure was maintained after applying the application.

Finally, I let the window-weld dry over night before removing the clamps and towels and removing the excess material with a scalpel.

It is still holding up great and there is no more water getting in the car. And might I add that we have had a couple.of nasty storms to test the repair.

At a price point 50% higher than many competing resins, this product had a lot of expectations to live up to; I was pleased to discover it delivers on the promise of a professional grade resin with a little extra resiliency. It prints using my normal settings in both my Photon Zero and Photon Mono X printers, and the results come out with nice detail just as you'd expect.

The main difference between this resin and others is that it has a little elasticity to it. Normal 3D printer resins have a bad habit of shattering at the slightest provocation; this product has a little bend to it, which is a really useful property for industrial prototyping. Most of my prints are for mechanical parts and I tend to have to plan for a limited lifespan when using 3D printing resins, so the extra resiliency more than pays for the cost increase.

It's still possible to shatter this resin - I had trouble removing one print from my build surface, and hacking away at it with a hammer and chisel caused it to shatter in the same way as every other normal resin I'm used to. But for stresses to a part on the margin, this seems a lot better than standard resins.

If you're just printing figurines or aesthetic parts to sit on a shelf, this probably isn't the resin you're looking for. But if you're working on mechanical parts and are looking for a step up from "ABS-like" resins, this is a unique option that could be worth the extra investment.

I've had this tool for about three months now. I originally purchased it for use in the automotive field, which has been my trade probably for more years than many of you have been alive. I'm sure most of you have used the basic handheld infra red thermometers that are out there on the market and found them to be pretty useful. All I can tell you is, when you use this tool for the first time, it'll put a smile on your face, from ear to ear. Seriously. It's like being able to see for the first time. The amount of info you can get from one image is amazing. Say for example, you suspect a radiator for an overheating problem. The old way you had to point at every square inch of the radiator and either write down all of the recordings or try and develop a mental picture of the hot or cold spots. With the VT02 I just take one snap shot and I'm done, saving a lot of time. And it's not just a time saver. It's hard to explain. You just start seeing things differently. I have information I never had access to before, but it was there all along. You start seeing different ways of diagnosing problems.
It also helps with sales. Ever had a car with a binding caliper? You try and sell the customer the full pop, right? Calipers, rotors, pads but they think you're scamming them and say, "Just do the pads..." Take a shot of both right and left calipers, and even a FEW degrees difference between calipers is noticeable. It's no longer the mechanic's opinion, it's hard data that you can print out or save as a .jpg file (it comes with software for reports and stuff) and show the customer. It's now in the customer's lap to make the common since decision to make the safe choice.
It's great for looking at A/C stuff, heater core inlet and outlet temps for checking for plugged heater cores. I could go on on on, but if you've been in the business a bit, you already know what you can use it for. That's why you're here, right? :) And the more you use it, the more things you think of to use it for.
Speaking of using it for different things- I brought it home to mess around with it. I also experiment with electronics projects as a hobby. In particular, my latest obsession has become the Arduino micro controller boards. I knew my board was getting hot, but the VT02 pinpointed it to the onboard voltage regulator @175F. The rated voltage input is up to 20vdc. My supply was at 15vdc but still got the thing stinkin' hot. Dropped the voltage and all is good. I also checked my home A/C and heating system with it.
Fluke is CRAZY rugged. I have a Fluke 88-V DMM that's ridiculous and the build quality of the VT02 looks to be of the same heritage.
It's got a built in lens protector so you'll never lose it. Comes with a microSD chip for storing images. I think it has a two year warranty. Comes with a nice soft case.

Pros-Amazing technology, first of it's kind that I know of in this price range
- Like they say, "A picture is worth a thousand words" (and maybe some money in your pocket)
- It's got this "thermal blending" mode that lets you blend the "regular" pic with a thermal pic which helps in clarifying what you're looking at.
-Real time on screen blue and red floating pixels to indicate max and min temps. This is very useful for radiators, condensers etc...
- Fluke build quality
-Color thermal image of problem area (beautiful color display)
-You can save images as file or print it out
-You'll be the envy of the shop, so they'll have to get their own, I will NOT loan this one out :)

Cons- The price may seem cost prohibitive for some at first, but it has the potential to pay for itself quickly. In this case, you DEFINITELY get what you pay for

There are many great reviews of this 3D printer, so I'll just offer some quick thoughts.

Overall, this is a very solid little printer. I'd buy it again.

DO NOT STORE IN GLASS. GALLIUM IS MESSY. (Further details in comments)

Shipping take about a week, maybe a few days longer. It ships from China, so that’s the speed you’d expect. Faster shipping would cost a LOT. I will not take any starts off for this shipping.

100g arrived as two tubes filled with 50g each (I haven’t weighed it but will later) the tubes have lids that are glued shut. Upon opening one lid broke away from the tube (due to cold I believe)

It’s exactly what it says, about 100g of gallium metal. This stuff is fun to play with but BEWARE! GALLIUM IS MESSY. It has strong wetting properties and is very soft when liquid. It will turn your hands black and stick to your table. BE CAREFUL.

Fun experiments: you can scratch aluminum and place a drop of gallium on top. The gallium will form an alloy with the aluminum that’s weak and the can will slowly crumble!

I put some gallium in a solution of copper sulfate and have had metallic copper precipitating from the solution as the gallium replaces the copper.

Soap and water is good for removing gallium from your hands, and I’ve found tissues rubbed on tables with a smooth surface can remove the gallium stain.

I transferred my gallium into a 2L soda bottle preform. The gallium coated the inside of the container so that you can not see where the gallium is from the outside.

Gallium expands as it cools just like water. Because of this, a glass container can shatter if gallium is allowed to cool inside. BE CAREFUL WHAT CONTAINER YOU CHOOSE.

OK, first I have to tell you that this is not my first go around with the A10M. The first one I had (which actually was my first Geeetech) left me somewhat miffed. I had many issues with it and eventually returned it and purchased an A10. I have been hooked on Geeetech printers ever since. I now realize that the A10M issues were through no fault of Geeetech’s, but my own.

So, here is my review of my second A10M.

This is definitely not a printer for neophytes. Sure, the setup, leveling and over-all running of the printer is relatively pain free, but to get the “perfect print” you have to do quite a bit of tweaking. And it really does not matter what slicer software you are using.

For lack of a better analogy, the A10M is an A10 on RedBull. It has all of the capabilities of the A10 but affords the user the added advantage of multicolor printing. Notice, I did not say “dual” color printing. That is because, with free software available via Geeetech and also options in certain slicer software, you can “mix” or “blend” the colors to create even more. This, in and of itself, makes for some very interesting and creative prints.

As you can see by the pictures, I am still learning. I have not gotten a print that I am 100% happy with, but that is because of my own lack of experience and nothing to do with the printer.

Not to sound like I am regurgitating my A10 review, but since they share so many of the same features, the pros and cons are very much in line with each other.

PROS:

· The printer is extremely easy to
build/setup.
· Multicolor / Free software from Geeetech
allowing color gradients, etc.
· The "Super Plate" provides good adhesion
but also, simple removal of prints.
· Bed leveling is easy (I decided to forego
any sort of leveling sensor, as they tend to
be troublesome).
· The "Old School" dial display is intuitive
(and to me more satisfying than a "touch
screen").
· Moderate build size (220*220*260), gives
ample print room.
· Power outage recovery feature is
awesome.
· Uses open source firmware.
· Has filament runout detection.
· Has a huge online user/support presence.
· Customer service / after purchase support
is incredible.
· ** THE PRICE **

CONS:

· Exposed LCD cable can get caught on
things (solved by printing drawer from
Thingiverse).
· SD card accessibility for people with fat
fingers. It is a full size card however.
· Open LCD back (solved by printing cover
from Thingiverse).
· Open fan ventilation (solved by printing
cover from Thingiverse).
· To get the “perfect” color print, many
tweaks are needed. I have yet to find a
profile for this printer for ANY slicer that
works 100% across the board.
· More prone to filament jams than other
printers because of the single head/multi
color setup.
· The filament holders are not positioned
“correctly” (changed the configuration).

All in all, I would say that this printer is awesome. If you don’t mind tweaking certain settings. I am sure that you will be able to produce some quality prints. That being said, even though I say that it is not for neophytes, I should rephrase that and say that it is not for neophytes that do not want to do some tweaking. :-)

I had a common problem with my Winnebago RV where the fresh water tank, when filling, would start dumping out of the 1/2" overflow pipe as it got full. Once this started, a siphon-effect would ensue and half the water that I'd just added to the tank would drain out. So it was impossible to get the fresh tank full.

Winnebago recommended that I install a larger (3/4") overflow tube right after the existing 1/2" tube turns down to drain, thus allowing the siphon to break. But that would have been a lot of work. Instead, I installed this valve near the top of the 1/2" tube - right where it comes out of the tank. Then I fiddled with it and got it to a point around the half-open position where it limited the water flow enough to allow that siphon to break without having to replace all of the overflow tubing.

The solution took me a few minutes and works like a charm.

I like it - it is smaller than I expected. Only criticism is true for pretty much any 3d printer I hear ... build plate adhesion. There is a bit of a learning curve to using it, but has been pretty good.. Some good prints. Some failures.

UPDATE: I've had this a few weeks now, For the price I'd say this is a great little printer. I've tried several kinds of filament with good results. The initial build plate yellow masking tape basically never worked for me. Could not print on it. Tried all the tricks I found online - hairspray, glue, changing temperature, releveling plate - none of that worked. Didn't really want to start off by modifying the printer (changing bed to glass etc). I pulled the original tape and used blue painters tape. Worked! Generally that seems to be the trick for me - have changed a couple of times when prints seem to stop sticking well and the tape looks pretty worn.(I've been printing a lot)
Then it jammed. Turned out to be my fault. Changing filament and the filament broke in the hot end (I didn't preheat enough to back filament out). Needed a 1.5 mm hex wrench to loosen so I could get the broken piece out. The hex nut is hidden behind the fan - the fan just unclips from the mounting on either side. re-fed filament in and it's fine again.
After about two weeks... suddenly could not print anything. Very frustrating! And I think I understand now. This printer is NOT ENCLOSED. Environment Matters! Do you have a breeze in the room (open windows)? Variation in room temperature? Ambient room temperature matters! No (nearby) open windows, and generally "warmer" ambient room temperatures seem to keep this running better.
The only real drawback I see to this printer is the build plate size -- it is simply too small to print some of the things I would like to try (Glow in the dark light switch plates seemed like a fun idea for the kids' rooms - but the build plate isn't large enough for that). I would still grab one of these printers - still a lot you can do. If the plate were bigger I'd give it 5 stars.
PS- the scrap of filament they include with the printer isn't enough to print much of anything (not even enough to complete the demo gcode file included. Make sure you buy a spool of filement to go with this!
REVISED- Have had this for a couple of months. One thing I would add: wiring to the heated build plate is not ideal. It runs inside and underneath- so motion of the build plate seems to wear this out and kink or break the wires over time. The heated build plate quit working on mine.Seems to be a known problem. Support was quick and courteous and they sent me a new plate with wiring attached. I have also seen mods online to rerun wires out the back instead of underneath the plate. Seems like that would last longer and should be easy to do.

This is the first 3d printer I have owned, but I've had the opportunity to use one several times at work. Granted, this printer is much smaller and lower cost than the one at work, but the prints turn out amazing. The best advice I can give to anyone buying an Ender 3 printer is setup is key. Take your time assembling it, paying close attention to making sure the X-axis gantry is as parallel to the base as you can. Carefully level the print bed. You may also need to adjust the part cooling fan slightly so it blows air at the bottom .065 inch of the nozzle. I rushed through assembling the printer, taking roughly 2 hours to put it all together and start printing, and got good results. After using it a few weeks, I went back and carefully adjusted everything to as tight of tolerance as I could, and the prints came out amazing! This printer is simple to use, and will handle PLA, PET-G, and ABS filament, thanks to the heated bed, and lends itself well to modification. If you want a 3d printer that won't break the bank and give you good prints, look no further. Not only will this printer suit you as a beginner into the world of 3d printing, it is readily adaptable as you grow from a beginner into a hobbyist.

I have been using the Qidi X-one 2 for a couple of years now having bought it on a whim with no previous knowledge of 3D printing or indeed design for 3D printing , so I thought it might be a good time to write something of my experience
I decided on the X-one 2 due to its very reasonable price and the fact it was all metal , looked sturdy and was fully enclosed thus eliminating need for a draft free environment that other open frame printers needed
It arrived in a sturdy box and only required the glazing panels to be installed and the bed levelled by following the supplied instructions for it to be ready to print, it came supplied with a drum of bright orange PLA which I eagerly installed and proceeded to try with a supplied test file and here is where I hit my first major snag as the movement of the spool on its mount allowed the filament to drop into the gap between the reel and the printer and jam, I solved this rather inelegantly by crushing a cardboard box with a hole in the middle to take up the slack and reprinted the test file successfully
My first design project was some large spacer washers of various thickness that I can mix and match to take up the gap on the reel mount instead of the cardboard box lol
Since then I have taught myself design principles using fusion 360 and using the Qidiprint software to slice the designs to enable printing, this software is so simple to set up and adjust it should be an industry standard , I have made parts for my motorcycle, parts to repair tools, even simple things like a little tray to hold components while I was building an electronic kit and of course the obligatory bust
The first two photos show the drawing and the final print of a part used to repair a ratchet spanner, the third picture shows the black collar made to reinforce a repair on the tray for an ice making machine, the forth picture shows the mounting bracket for the sat nav fitted to my bike and the fifth picture is the obligatory bust
The printer has performed faultlessly except when I make mistakes like the time I blocked the nozzle by failing to back the filament out far enough to ensure clean removal but an email to Qidi elicited complete information how to remove the blockage in less than 24 hours and indeed any questions I have had have been answered with the same efficiency every time no matter how stupid the question was
I would have no hesitation in recommending these printers and indeed the company to anyone

I take pride in having an oil stain free driveway. Visitors to my home don't usually feel the same way.
I caught their leak on the same day but it had been parked and dripped for a few hours already. The immediate treatment and spray brake cleaner and grind in "oil dri" absorbant usually does a decent job if was treated immediately. But because this time it was left for hours, the stain was still there, this was a royal purple oil because it was a very dark purple stain.

I found this on amazon and was hoping this product really works or lighten the stain. I left it on for a week, it is very hot during this time and I kept applying moisture about 3-4 times a day but it would probably dry out in an hour. The consistency of the product is a very light powder but after wetting it and drying out it does not get blown out by wind.

After straight 7 days of treatment, I decided to rinse it off to see the progress. I am happy to say it is almost completely gone. Oil stain is very easy to see when you wet the concrete but it is even hard to see under wet concrete. I had to mark where the very faint spot is so I could come back and reapply the product. I own many different kinds of cleaner and also a pressure washer. In my opinion pressure washer will remove some but also push the oil deep into the pores so I do not recommend it. This product uses a bacteria is smaller than the pores in the concrete and consumes it. It really saved my driveway and these visitors will be asked to park far and away next time.

This review is for the shining purple to luminous green petg filament printed using prusa with .4 nozzle.
Like the title says, this filament was challenging for me to dial in. Eventually I found flawless results using a very clean textured steel sheet. According to many reviews and the filament label I was under the impression that this filament would print best at lower temps 215°c - 220°c, for me these temps inevitably lead to bubbling, stringing and the filament failing to adhere to the heat bed. Eventually after several hours of fine tuning and frustration, I found that increasing the mesh bed leveling to 7x7, increasing the nozzle temp to 250°c and the heat bed to 85-90°c and calibrating the first layer, I was finally able to achieve a flawless print with very minimal stringing. I am now very happy with the final results of this filament and would recommend this product to anyone interested in this color. The glow does not last long and charges best with uv lighting but the shinning purple is a slightly translucent and a very nice color to add to my collection. Final prints seem strong and durable.

I have recently found myself having to strip a lot of automotive paint and rust in the process of restoring some vintage cars. Along the way I have found different forms of the non-woven abrasive tools that do a great job, including drums for my burnishing tool. These disc for an angle grinder are the missing piece in my paint stripping/metal finishing tool kit. The burnishing drums are great for large flat surfaces, but can't get into lips, and sharper contours. The discs on an angle grinder take care of those areas and more. It makes short work of stripping the paint off of a wheel well lip and I was able to strip half of a rear fender in just a few minutes. I also have a firewall section that is covered with adhesive from a heat shield and the disc is making quick work of removing the glue and the paint.
So far the disc seems to wear well, in that after stripping an entire fender the disc showed very little wear. I did have to remove the disc guard from my grinder as the disc did make contact with it. I also had to flip over the retaining nut on the spindle in order to be able to tighten down on the disc, as that section of the disc is thinner than a standard grinding disc. You will also want to wear a mask when using the stripping disc as they do create a lot of very find air born debris that isn't the best thing to be breathing.

I received this endoscope to test and review.

This endoscope is nicely packaged and seems built well. I don't know how many drops the hand unit could take, but it feels well constructed. It assembles in a minute or so, very simple, and you can have it up running to do a variety of searches and recoveries.

The camera is very tiny and you are not going to get high def video out of it, but I think that a good thing haha. Some of the things you'll see with this, going into walls and pipes, you really don't want to see in HD. :)

You can flip the screen any time on the control panel in case the camera gets turned around while moving it through tight spaces. It has an SD card slot so you can record and take pictures for reference. The camera has LED lights on the end so you'll be able to see in those dark places.

The cable is both stiff and flexible giving you the ability to move around corners while also still being able to move it vertically. The camera is waterproof so using it to find lost or dropped items in pipes and other tight places. It comes with attachments so you can grab lost things or remove small obstructions. There's a magnet, a hook and a mirror to look around corners. Very nice add ons. It also have a flash light on the main body that is nice and bright.

Overall this is a nice endoscope and will be very helpful to have around the house, even for non professionals.

The knobs that were replaced appear to have been original and after 70 years these new knobs look almost identical with only minor differences. Most notably is that the line indicator on the old ones are painted in an inset groove while the new ones are just painted on the surface. I'm hoping the indicator doesn't easily get worn off. Note that these are the 1500AU. The AU and AV variants which I see are both selling on Amazon have the line indicator, but the ones just labeled 1500 with no letters after don't have a line indicator according to the datasheet. If in doubt just check the Davies Moulding 1500 datasheet page and check for the "indicator line" column.

I use double-sided tape for my CNC projects. I bought this to try out because I needed a thinner type of tape than I had been using. This tape is beautiful for what I'm doing.

I primarily work with wood and most double sided tape, though holds really good, also releases harshly and has a high chance of tearing the wood or leaving unwanted marks or glue.

The first time I tried this I was worried because it seemed it wasn't sticking well enough and my piece was going to move in the machine. That was a simple fix once I quit using it like my old tape. I just needed to be sure to apply even pressure, kind of like I needed to activate it and remove the tiny bubbles so it would stick better. It reminds me of a product I used for vinyl that moved and released really well because of a similar feature of tiny air pockets. So I was able to move the tape in place easily and once I pressed on it by just running my thumb along it it was holding very well.

I haven't had a piece move yet and every time I'm done and peel it off there's little to no residue.

My power supply adaptor is located outside the house but safe from the elements and I installed the resistor right next to it. It looks neat. It would definitely look ugly if the resistor is connected to the ring device itself and also adds additional risk of exposer to the elements. So, it would make more sense to connect the resistor close to the transformer/power adaptor side. I cut one of the wires close to the power adaptor end and connected the resistor in between, so I ended up with the resistor out of sight. In other words, electrically it does not matter where in the circuit the resistor is connected - directly on the ring device or close to the adaptor. What is important is that there's a resistor between one of the wires leading off the ring device and going into the power adaptor. I believe most users would opt for this configuration I've used.

Converted one of my turkey fryers to Natural Gas for homebrewing. This thing heats up water in a hurry. It brought 8 gallons of 55-degree water up to 170 degrees in about 20 minutes. After mashing, it brought a 5-gallon batch to a boil in about 15 mintues; a 10-gallon batch (14 gal mashed wort) up to a boil in about 30-40 minutes. This thing's going to save so much time on brew day. I'll be converting my other brew stand to natural gas after working with this.

I have a Sony Gold headset for console gaming (PS4) that, despite its bad press, I am rather fond of. But, one of its drawbacks is indeed durability - the plastic along the entire length of the headband is prone to cracking, especially the plastic along the hinges above the ear cups. It's a common issue, so common that Sony has ceased coverage of this damage type under their warranty. And lo, my headset cracked a hinge, the other hinge on the verge, and stress fractures formed along the length of band near my temple. But i really like this headset so i decided to salvage it.

One suggestion for fixes were using epoxy or its variants. Which i tried, and it lasted maybe a week. Epoxy is more like an industrial glue, but most glues, honestly, don't do jack unless you plan on never touching that item again. The only glue that has ever worked was Elmer's glue over 20 yrs ago, and only if gluing paper to paper. Another suggestion mentioned silicon fusing tape, wherein the tape doesn't stick in the traditional sense, but rather sticks to itself quite readily, and never lets go. After browsing a few different brand names, i decided on Rescue Tape.

I began wrapping the two main problem areas (broken hinge and fractured temple). Getting the tape started was a bit of a hassle, as i should've secured the headset to something first. This tape indeed did not stick to anything but itself. Held the end of the roll in place and stretched the tape as long as physically able, then wrap, then stretch, etc. I just followed the directions, basically. Check out my photo for the end result. It's not pretty but it holds.

I don't know what's happening on the molecular level, but this stuff adheres to itself like white on rice. I bought this to check for hot/cold spots in my house. It works better than expected. I found a wall that has a hot section due to a hole in the subfloor where a drain pipe passes through. I could also see the area in the attic where I forgot to replace the insulation after remodeling the kitchen.
I can see where the studs are through the sheetrock. You can also see where some of the ducting is for the HVAC system. I can actually see where a flexible vent tube snakes across a bedroom ceiling.
You need to figure out what color scheme works best for the situation. For some of the choices the colors are relative. Looking at a wall from one direction shows different colors than looking at the same wall with other objects in view. As long as you know this the colors make more sense.
I did use it outside a few times too. It's cold outside where I am. I walked out to the sidewalk and looked back at the house. It showed up in brilliant colors. You can pick out all windows, doors and light fixtures.
I also went for a walk in the woods to see what I could see. Not a lot of wildlife out at night. I was able to spot a few rabbits at 30 40 yards. You only see a small heat signature as they are well insulated. I don't know what a larger animal might look like. It runs off you phones battery so probably not good to use for night vision type work.
Overall I'm happy with the purchase. It does what I need it to.

Look, you get what you pay for but with that said, this kit can deliver to an average DIY’er. If you’re looking for industrial use or even moderately heavy use, go with something a bit more expensive. But comparing this to even “middle” tier Irwin kit, it’s on par. Proper understanding and use is critical to not only this kit, but any kit you buy. You need to make sure you use the proper sized drill bit for your hole, understand how different metals and their thickness can impact the tool itself, use proper cutting oil, go slow and these will work just fine. We use Klutch brand taps at my job and we tap metals from 3/16in all the way to 1 1/2in thick and tap holes as large as 5/8-11.  We use a pneumatic tap arm so it’s less work for us but guess what? Those expensive little taps break on us all the time too. As for the case issue people complained of. Mine came in great shape and in order. I’ve messed around with it jiggling it and flipping it and only a couple of the smaller taps have came loose inside the case. For a homeowner/DIY’er, this kit is the best bang for your buck.

I have 10 printers in total from different brands and have always bought the latest and greatest hype. With the anycubic i3 Mega this was not the case. I was looking to get a new printer that I could have on the desk at my home instead of the office with all the others. For this I looked into different aspects, it had to be compact in size but also have a big build volume. And also it had to be packaged in the best possible way because it would get re shipped from miami to Guatemala (our mail is not exactly the best at taking care of packages) and I would not have a chance to return it if I had any problems.
So first packaging:
-It comes well protected in quality cardboard and styrofoam. The box took a beating and still everything on the printer worked
Assembling:
-The printer comes almost assembled, you just have to put 8 screws and you are done.
First usage:
- It comes preloaded with a model (the owls in the picture) the model prints at an awesome quality, you just have to level the print bed before
Noise:
- This is something that is not mentioned in a lot of reviews and I think it's something most people don't take into account when buying their first
3d printer. The i3 mega is fairly quiet for its size and even when printing at 60mm/s I could still sleep with no problems
Build quality:
- As I mentioned before, the build quality is superb, the all metal frame is really sturdy and you won't have any problems with it
Print quality (pictures attached, this is direct from the printed without any processing):
PLA: its prints it great out of the box with no problem, I tried different PLA brands and they all worked great (dragon, piramid, candy monster)
PETG: the first prints where a little tricky but after some tweaking on simplify3d it prints it at a great quality ( Elastic Top Gun!)
ABS: it takes a while to get the print bed to 100C (around 8 minutes) but after that it prints it with a good quality the ultrabase does a great
work at sticking everything to the bed ( Pikachu, lithophane)
TPU: this material is elastic so not many printers will print it without any modifications and to my surprise the i3 Mega does. It takes some test
prints to achieve that other modified printers get but this one does it without any mods. ( Go Pro mount on quad, GoPro mount)
-Will it last?
So this is something everybody questions when they are buying an electronic from a company that is in Asia will it last or will it break after a month of usage. I have been using this printer for 6 months almost on a daily basis and it still prints great. In this time I only had two problems, first was that I had to change the hot end (Anycubic does add a spare one on the box, no other company does this) and the other problem that I had was that the print bed was warped (I emailed support, they asked me to send them some photos of the problem and after 3 emails they shipped me a complete bed assembly at no cost to me. So trust me their support is one of the best)
- Community
The i3 Mega has a great community of users behind it always trying new stuff and doing mods to it, there are groups on facebook and in other
forums if you ever want to try something different or just talk to other people that have the same printer. Also don't be scared that you wont get
support both anycubic support and the community are great.

To summarize:

The good:
-Great build quality
-Can print TPU,PLA,PETG,ABS (I only tried these maybe it can print others)
-Great support from Anycubic
-Not noisy compared to other printers
-Can withstand 6 months of almost daily use
- Easy to use interface
- Big build volume compared to the size it takes on a desk

The bad:
-Its heavy to move around from place to place, but the small volume makes this easy

CA glue generally cures fast except when you really need it to. I've seen YouTube makers using CA activator to get faster results so when this package showed up on Amazon, I decided to try it. I put glue on one piece of wood and activator on the other then put them together. The instructions said it might take up to a minute to cure but it was instant in my test. After the two pieces of wood were joined (about three square inches of overlap, I tried to separate them - I wasn't going to happen.
The activator is a thin, watery liquid and the glue is a gel which wasn't at all runny. My only caveat for this product is that you really need to position your parts accurately first try, because you won't get to reposition them after they tough. Good stuff.

I bought my first Gorilla Cart at Costco and used it for carting everything from boxes of books to bags of compost. It is amazingly sturdy, and never feels like it is wobbly or unstable. The locking rear wheels make it easy to load heavy or bulky stuff without the cart rolling away. And it folds down flat enough that I can stow it away against the wall in the garage when I am not using it.

I have two complaints:

1) the small front wheels do not turn, so if you are rolling the cart with the front wheels down, you have to yank it to make it turn. The solution is to tilt the cart back and wheel it like a dolly, but it would have been nice if the front wheels turned so that you could steer it when it is flat.

2) the reason I am on my second cart is my rat of a brother borrowed the first one when he was moving, and it is now permanently at his apartment 300 miles away. The lesson here is not to let anyone use your cart, and if they ask to use it tell them that it is just a cheap cart and you are worried about how hard it will be for them to use it (because it is so easy to use and conveniently fits in any car so that they can take off with it, leaving you to buy a new cart).

Overall, this is a great cart that is well designed and can handle heavy and bulky loads with ease.

So, I have to say, for the price I bought this at I expected it to be kinda crappy.  However, after finally getting the instructions off the CD onto a tablet, building this thing was a breeze for me and my wife.  I do have a couple things to say about that though.  First off, the directions for assembly.  There wasn't a lot of writing in them other than what nuts and bolts to use at what time.  On that note, however, the color pictures were extremely helpful.  My wife and I only messed up 4 times during the build, and it is our first 3d printer.  The first and, in my opinion most notable, error was right in the beginning.  The large acrylic frame is made of three pieces.  We reversed the sides of the two back pieces and didn't realize until we had finished the build and were wiring the thing.  So our control board and power supply are reversed.  This actually caused a flub in our wiring (my fault) and we broke the wires on one of the stop switches (also easily fixed....mostly).  When we were adjusting the bed and z-stop, we went too low and put a scratch in the corner of the print bed.  The last error was in the Y axis motor.  The belt was a little too loose and shook on of the holding screws on the pulley out and jammed the motor.  Easily fixed.  The only gripe I had in the build was the making of the filament stand.  It comes with one that is fairly simple to assemble and mounts on top of the frame.  It may have been sturdy, but the laser cut on it was slightly off and it wouldn't mount to the frame at all.  I plan to print off a different one anyway so no loss there.  All in all, it's a decent printer and is currently printing our test build from the cd.  Despite the terrible and not so terrible flubs in building and starting the dang thing up, it was a very forgiving build and I would recommend this printer to anyone as a first build....well....anyone that has experience in building electronics, that is.

The Creality Ender line of printers is wonderful for the money (I have three of them), but they often suffer from beds that are wavy or warped. An example is my Ender-3 S1 Pro which, fortunately, came with CR Touch auto leveling.

If you print on glass, that's not so much of a problem as the glass won't take on the shape of the bed underneath. But if you print on PEI-covered steel sheets held on magnetically, a less-than-flat bed can make it hard to get a good first layer. That's where this comes in. With CR Touch, the printer firmware can run tests of the bed height at 25 locations (5 x 5 array), building a model of the variations so that it can correct for them with minute adjustments to the Z-axis to compensate. That can make all of the difference in the world as to whether a print is successful or loses bed adhesion.

The kit includes the CR Touch sensor, a cable, three zip-ties, four screws, and three brackets. Don't worry -- you will only need to use one of the brackets, with the other two being for use on other printers. Installation is quite simple with the hardest part being the routing of the wiring, which isn't particularly hard on most of the Ender printers.

I recommend first leveling the bed manually and then using the CR Touch sensor to assist you in fine tuning the leveling knobs to achieve maximize flatness. Five or six runs should be all that it takes to make the necessary fine adjustments. Remember, three points defines a plane, so four-point, spring-loaded leveling can actually warp the surface if the leveling nuts are not adjusted with near perfection.

For many years i had seen this device. Read reviews, looked form far, but my cintiq 21ux gave me almost accurate colors, so for e was a waste of money. So ive skip it. I was talking about the old one spyder pro 2 or 3. I think it was 2.

Now, after i bought the cintiq 22hd, with more brightness and more contrasti got color blinded. Having too much can be bad, new monitors they have the brightness so wayyyy up, that you can almost lit a room.

Noticed that the default 6500k in rgb was a bit different from my old cintiq, i saw the flesh tones and said, ummmmmm. Must be a wrong color profile. Then some friends of mine complained my colors looked really dark, i mean almost black. So i had to tone down the brightness on my monitor.

Do some test, and noticed that looks good on my cintiq, but bad on my second screen, a dell monitor. Also in the ipad looked dark and in my cellphone looked sooo bright?

So i was shooting in the dark.

Then the spyder 4pro cath my attention, this time has 7 sensors for different tones of blues, and even a light room sensor, to callibrate the light of the monitor with the room. Again why should i spend 140 dollars, maybe it wont work.

So ive skip it, until a friend with same cintiq model brought it, and say it was awesome.

So it was decided i bought it.

I followed the instructions. Was really easy, took me a while to notice i had to press continue, hhahaha i was waiting like almost an hour. hahhahahahahhahah

But then after ten minutes of calibration my heart was beating fast, did it was a success?, How wrong i had my monitor calibrated? Will it calibrate a second screen? Will i have trouble like other people that gave it a one star?

Then i clicked next. Then i got dissapointed that didnt changed the tones like from night to day, but after my second blink of my eyes, like they refreshed the image, i was like WOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWWW what the hell?

The flesh tones looked so real from photos, so i looked my reference images and photos looked amazing, i can even notice tiny details, that couldnt see on the image before. By default the new cintiq 22hd in 6500k mode, the flesh tones looked like yelloew with blues, now they look warm and real.

I was surprised that the spyderpro also detected the dell, and i was able to calibrate both screens, the dell has more contrast becaus eits a better monitor. But now they look almost the same. I was like hell yeahhhhh.

I noticed i could calibrate my ipad too, so i downloaded the program and a nother HEEELLLLL YEEEAHHH.

I dont regret a single penny spend on this one, my lazyness and indesition made me choose the wrong colors all this time, hope that now the colors look more wamr,at least to my eyes.

I purchased this for a V2.4 350mm 3d printer build that I had recently converted to a water cooled dragon hotend and wanted to have a water temp sensor so i could monitor the temps of the cooled portion of my hotend. The thermistor does exactly that but if your using klipper with the standard two thermistors, one for the hotend and one for the bed(and your using a BTT octopus like i am), you then need to set on your klipper config a new temperature sensor, i copied the hotend temp sensor macro then pasted it and changed the name to [temperature_sensor water_temp] and the pin is set to the next avalible which will be "sensor_pin: PF5" if you have not already added another sensor, one of the most important parts is changing sensor type(if acplicable) to "sensor_type: NTC 100K MGB18-104F39050L32" this is what this sensor functioned best on and provided the most accurate results, i used twi thermistors and gave them both the same exact temperature, I tried this with various sensor types and "NTC 100K MGB18-104F39050L32" was the overall best. so if your like me and needed a new sensor or have purchased this for printer running klipper, I recommend you use "NTC 100K MGB18-104F39050L32" for the sensor type

I purchased two of these 145# neodynium "Manic" brand magnets for miscellaneous shop use. These magnets have a tremendous pulling force and when they lock together it is a real challenge to separate them! The magnet's surrounding body is a high quality plated steel. The Outside Diameter is ~ 1 9/16" and there is a counter sunk hole in the pulling face large enough to accept at least a #10 screw for attaching it to a mounting point like a wall, ceiling or a pick-up pole. The pulling force is directed to the counter sunk face of the magnet; the force is much lower on the reverse face. In my attached photo the pulling face is on the left side where the countersunk hole is located.

If you have a need for strong and easily mounted magnets these will do a great job for you. I received a discount on one of the magnets for providing this honest and unbiased review. I will purchase more when I need them.

I bought this 30 gallon plastic drum Eagle 1601MB Blue High Density Polyethylene Lab Pack Drum which comes with a tapered lid that nicely seals the drum to use as a dust collector in my woodshop. I cut a hole in the lid with a hole saw on my drill and mounted an [[ASIN:B002JP315K Oneida Molded DIY Dust Deputy Cyclone]] on it. I then made a two shop vacuum y-adapter out of dust collection parts that I hook up to two shop vacuums when I use my planer. I use my planer infrequently (maybe once a month) so it is not a big deal to use the two shop vacs. One shop vac is dedicated to my saw (on a relay) so it goes on automatically--I use a five gallon dust seperator model CV-06 from Clear View Cyclones--this dust collector is easy to open and empty and just sits next to the shop vac. I steal this away temporarily from table saw. The 30 gallon system is only used when I use the planer as it is easier to use and works better than the "trash can sock" attachment that DeWalt sells for use with the planer. My wife and I are very happy with the 30 gallon drum method. We do not use the steel clamp to hold the lid on as it is unneccessary. If I ever have a lot of water to pick up, the drum would be handy for that also. If I can remember, I will take a couple of pictures and put them on my own website (I think Amazon does not allow me to post pictures anymore). I'll update this description if I accomplish this task.

I made the mistake of only noting there was film on one side of the plastic, when the directions said to remove the film, so was surprised the it was much cloudier than the reviews said. Removing the second side after I used it, I was pleased to see it is clear with no cloudiness.  It is tricky to even note there is film on the plastic as there are no tabs to pull it off and it is cut exactly on and flush with the plastic, however, peeling down from the corner it was easy to remove. I had someone sitting behind me who talked throughout one flight, so I had wished for better side coverage, but that’s not really the intent of this. In working with clients in front of me, it would be good front coverage.  I have a pretty small face and head, but the shield has an comfortable adjustable strap on both sides, so that aspect should adjust to almost any size head.  Because it’s a lightweight plastic it can be marred easily. Someone bumped into it while I was holding it and it left a little line/crease. Its still useable, but I want to check with the company to see if they sell replacement plastic sheets for it, if it gets more banged up.  Although it was more expensive than many of the face shield on Amazon, it looks better made. I appreciated that it is not only made in the US, but in Bellevue, WA, which is local for me. Came much sooner than noted on purchase, likely because of my close proximity to the manufacturer.

As others have mentioned in their reviews this crystal is not as large as the listing photo would lead you to think, however it is pretty much the size that they describe in the product details. Mine arrived measuring 1-1/2 X 1-1/8 X 7/16 inches.
I wanted this to demonstrate the optical properties of Iceland Spar and how it may have been the mythical Viking Sun Stone which they were said to have used to navigate. It is excellent for that demonstration being quite optically clear with relatively few flaws, no huge inclusions, and it exhibits the phenomena quite well.

To use as a Sun Stone you place a small dot on one of the large faces. Use a marker or a teeny tiny piece of painter's tape. The dot wants to be quite small so before you go marking up your crystal with indelible ink try the tape. Hold the crystal up above your head so that the other large flat face is towards you ( marked face towards the sky) and about in plane with the sun. Look through the crystal as you rotate it about the axis which keeps the large flat faces in plane with the sun. You will see two dots from your side of the crystal. They change in density as you rotate it. When the density of both is equal one edge of the crystal is pointing toward the sun. This is supposed to work even on cloudy days when you can't actually see the sun, or just before sunrise or after sunset when the sun is below the horizon. It actually only seems to work if the background behind the stone is a patch of blue sky. If the background light is diffused through a layer of cloud the dots do not change density at all. However the sun can be behind a cloud just as long as you have a little patch of blue behind the stone.

It is said the Vikings used this property to determine the direction to the sun even when it could not be seen and by that means were able to maintain a sense of direction. No one explains that the Viking navigator would need a time piece to really make that system work, nor what they may have used for such a time piece, though an hour glass might have served well enough. Did Viking ships have hour glasses? I don't know.

Though never mentioned in literature it also seems to work in the other orientation, which is probably more useful to the navigator. That is you hold the wide flat surface perpendicular to the ground, one edge of the crystal pointed in the direction to the sun, dot side away from you. Now change the tilt until the two dots are equal density. This gives you the angle from horizontal to the sun along the top edge of the crystal. It is said that this can be accurate to within 1 degree with practice. If that is so it might allow a navigator to get a rough noon sight on marginal days when regular sextants wouldn't work because of the sun being obscured.

The phenomina is not as apparent if there is a lot of scattered light about, such as when indoors where the sun light is bouncing off numerous walls. Also the effect is completely spoiled if the sky behind the stone as you are looking at it is cloud covered thereby diffusing hte sunlight.

This is BY FAR my favorite filament I've purchased thus far (Galaxy Black). I've already gone through two spools of this stuff and I've only been 3D printing for a few months. This stuff just prints with absolutely no issues at all. Love it!

I am using this on my Prusa i3 MK3S, with the default Prusament PLA filament profile (215C nozzle, 60C bed). Most of my stuff was printed at 0.2mm layer height with the default PrusaSlicer settings.

Pros:
*This stuff HIDES LAYER LINES! Did I mention it hides layer lines? I mean, even at 0.20mm layer height, the tiny glitter particles masks the layer lines incredibly well.
*I've had very good success with this filament. Never had issues with jamming, or problems with the PLA containing too much moisture right out of the bag. I've had issues with other brands!
*Prusa goes to every extent to make their products extremely precise. You can measure the filament diameter for yourself and you will see that not a lot of other filaments are as precise as this stuff. They even have a report of the diameter of your exact filament as it was being wound onto the spool. Simply scan the QR code on the side of the spool and it will give you the report! What other filament brand does that?
*I have never seen a more beautifully wound spool of filament than the Prusament brand. When you open the vacuum sealed bag (which is reusable by the way!), you will notice how perfect the filament is wound up. If you've ever had a print get ruined because the filament spool getting tangled, then you know how frustrating this can be. Not something you have to worry about with the Prusament brand. For people with OCD like me, you will love the winding of this filament! It's perfect!

Cons:
*This stuff is expensive! At $30 bucks a spool, this is more expensive than most other PLA you can purchase on Amazon.
*At times (when sold out) this stuff can be very difficult to get your hands on. I usually order 2 spools at a time since when they are sold out, it can take up to a month or more before Amazon receives another shipment of Prusament brand filaments directly from Prusa himself. They have a pretty small filament production line, so when it's out, it takes a little while for them to ship more pallets to Amazon from the Czech Republic.

Overall:
I love this stuff. It's a huge upgrade from the silver stuff that came with my printer and I think what makes it stand above all of the other filaments I've used is how well it can hide layer lines. I love this stuff and would highly recommend it. Only bad thing about it is how quickly I run out of this stuff!

Great filament, different than I expected.

Filament color appears dark charcoal color, almost black on the spool, but when stringing it through a 0.4mm hardened nozzle and holding it up into the sunlight, it actually appears to be a clear filament with carbon strands in it, so it prints like a dark charcoal, not black.

The material itself doesn’t have a description aside from 3D Filament Carbon Fiber, and although the Amazon description says PLA and it prints within PLA temp ranges, the end item acts different as it isn’t as brittle as other PLA’s I’ve used.

The layer adhesion was really good, far better than expected. Single layer wall did separate at the layer line, but it took some bending and pulling. 4 layer base didn’t separate or rip. It took a bit of effort to bend it and although I was able to bend it, it wound up folding without breaking... showing great layer adhesion, but also an interesting flexing. I believe when printing an actual piece, it will be very stiff and durable, so don’t consider this filament flexible, but rather more “impact resistant” than other PLA’s which are typically more brittle (by my personal experience).

This test piece was a small piece, 20mm diameter x 5mm high ring/cup with a solid bottom... 4 layer base, single wall for the remaining print, no top.

I’ll update this review if I find anything I don’t like about the filament when I print in larger scale of production pieces... but just based off of this initial small torture test piece, I’m impressed!

I bought these to replace the worn-out original steel bearings on my vintage Microsoft USB Trackball Explorer (model X08 1.0 MS Trackball Explorer for PS2/USB, 46mm ball).. You wouldn't expect the plastic trackball to wear down steel bearings, but it's the dust from your hands that ends up wearing a flat spot on the bearings. The flat spots lead to sticky ball motion within a year or two of use.

I just carefully pried out the old balls with a pin, then pressed the new ones into the sockets with my finger. Took all of 5 minutes. 2mm (0.0787") is exactly the right size. You could also use synthetic sapphire balls which are basically the same thing as ruby except they're clear. Ruby can shatter and won't carry anything like the kinds of loads that steel or zirconia can, but that's just not a factor when the load is just a 2 ounce plastic trackball.

The trackball's action is now better than the new trackball ever was because ruby has no "grain," as opposed to steel which has a very fine grain structure like microscopic concrete that causes some drag on the ball. These ruby balls have even smoother action than the fancy zirconia ceramic bearings I've tried in the past.

The big news is that, two years of heavy use later, there's no sign whatsoever of wear on the balls and the action is still better than new. I don't expect to ever replace these since the ruby is much harder than any dirt or dust particles (except for ruby or diamond dust).

Update: After 3 years, the Trackball's action deteriorated and I found small flat spots! Still, 3 years is much better than the original steel balls. I just pried the balls out and put them back in, making sure the flat spots were face down. Works like new, again.

Update: Someone asked if the harder ruby bearings scratch the plastic trackball. No. Trackball is still perfectly glossy looking after all these years. Anything that runs smoother will also cause less wear, and these rubies are glass-smooth. Also, I'd expect less wear caused by ruby balls than steel since the steel balls get worn by dust, and that worn area will be rough, gouged & jagged steel at the microscopic level. Also, Elcom introduced their new huge ball trackball which runs on... synthetic ruby bearings.

The Toolant (1/8" - 5/32" - 3/16" - 1/4" ) step drill is excellent for the steepest shape tangs. I tried it on Maple, and it worked perfectly. I am very impressed by the sharpness of the drill, and I believe that it will also excel in cutting into metals.

Suggest turning of furnace until air circulating blower starts. Turn down thermostat. The hot air blower will continue automatically until it has reached it's cutoff point. This step is to apply heat to speed up high temperature silicon gasket maker curing.

Moly 25
Phosphorus 120
Zinc 10
Antimony 64

Vi @ 100c 220

The Antimony is an ester based anti wear additive. Schaeffer's refers to Molybdenum as micron Moly. Good stuff!

To be fair, I have never owned a 3D printer previously, but seeing reviews and comments on the Ender 3 series, I took a chance on the Ender 3 Pro, since the price was right.

Out of the box, I had it completely assembled in probably about a half hour or so, but that might've been aided by having watched a bunch of YouTube videos before it arrived. The only issues I had during installation, were making sure my cabling wasn't stuck behind the uprights before mounting them, and the little t-nuts that slide in the channel - some of them seem to want to spin inside, regardless of how careful you are with getting them in the proper orientation. Likewise, the spool holder is supposed to go on last, but if you do that, you can't try to line those up because of that issue. I removed the two bolts on the header from one end to slide the holder in, and then refastened. Not a major issue by far.

Printing is wonderful on this. I do have a level desk, and took time to level the bed. My first print was a shim for the X-motor for alignment as suggested by multiple reviews I had read and watched. I thought maybe I was a tiny bit too low, so I readjusted, and went too far. Next print wouldn't stick. Definitely a balancing act, but I went back down and then printed the included dog file, which printed flawlessly.

A few things I saw mentioned in prior reviews or videos, were things like the entry opening for the filament into the extruder, possibly wearing out over time. Also, the tube pulling away, some have said their bed was loose, or the belts were. Pleasantly, I found mine included clips for the tube already so I didn't have to print my own, and a metal sleeve where the filament feeds in. I still will print a guide later just for the path of it to be more natural, but I won't have to worry about wear. The files included on the card were pleasant - my version came with a dog, cat, pig, vase, heart-shaped box, and even Mjolnir.

With the vast support network of users (I can't speak for customer service but many people say that's not something to count on), and the wide variety of upgrades if one chooses, I am more than pleased with the purchase. Took the time to level the bed, calibrate the extruder (even though it might not be needed, I wanted to, to get the hang of it), and it's working wonderful, and really makes you just want to keep printing things!

I have several air cleaners in my house, and I recommend them highly. But, I was a bit lost as to exactly to what degree they were improving the air quality in my house...I had no way of really knowing. I also found the filter replacement times somewhat vague. You replace them based on keeping track of how many hours you have run your air cleaner at a given fan speed--the higher the fan speed, the fewer total hours of run time until you need to change each filter. This does not seem like the best way of knowing when to replace these costly items.

Doesn't it make sense that if there is not so much dust in your house, but a lot of dust in someone else's house, that running an identical air cleaner for the same amount of time and fan speed as the people in the other house is going to mean that your filters are not going to be plugged up as quickly as theirs? And, in order to save energy on the electric bill, how do I know what is the lowest fan speed to use to actually keep my air clean, given the size of my room and the actual dust that it contains or that flows into the room from doors and windows?

I started doing some research online and eventually came across this device.
I bought one of these Dylos air quality monitors and now that I am using it, I couldn't imagine running good air cleaners without one. It gives you an immediate readout of the quantity of particles floating around in your air, and a scale to tell you what that means. It allows you to see what is going on in your room, with your air cleaner, with your dust problem at this moment as it is affected by the outside air currents, etc.. This will make it possible to determine the best fan speed, and also allows you to tell the condition of your filters by measuring the clean air output of your air cleaner. You replace your filters when they are not filtering properly anymore, not when some arbitrary timer tells you to. I can move the Dylos from room to room to check, as it is small and light.
For the small cost of this device relative to electric costs and filter costs, it is a steal in the long run. I have no affiliation with Dylos. They have been well reviewed elsewhere and make the most reasonable particle counter on the market. It works for me, and I just thought I'd pass it along.

I bought this after I bought the one just like it but with the 5/8" nozzle. The smaller nozzle took too long to fill the things I wanted to use it for (riding lawn mower, ATV, boat) and since they all had large fuel supply holes I got this (I understand I will need the 5/8" for cars or the smaller garden tools). I am very happy with the quality. My husband filled both tanks at a gas station a half hour away and I couldn't even tell that they had been in the car.

We had been using the plastic containers, which made the car stink for days. I also hated to have to unscrew the nozzle, turn it around (getting gas on my hands) and try to get the nozzle in the lawnmower tank without spilling anything. This requires you squeeze a handle before the gas is released, the same idea as a gas pump, so nothing spills. It also feels much safer than the plastic tanks.

The only downside of these versus the plastic is the weight. They do weigh considerably more. Once I add 5 gallons of gas they get heavy. That is why I got this 1" nozzle version as it takes less time before the gas is transferred.

I met a representative from IC3D at the 2014 Midwest RepRap festival. I arrived late to the show otherwise I could have gotten some of the filament he was giving out to people. A lot of the machines there were running their filament and testing it out as it was a newer company at the time and all their prints looked pretty good and everyone seemed pleased with it. After finishing off my backlog of Sainsmart and SeeMeCNC filament I ordered some of this. I tested the filament diameter with my digital calipers and the tolerances are pretty good. I do average around 1.75mm +/-. I was hoping to order some white PLA but at this time they are only selling black and this natural colored PLA filaments. They do carry a variety of ABS colors. This natural filament is more clear, like glass. I'm running it through a .4mm nozzle with a .2963mm layer height at 220C and have absolutely no issues.

My only complaint is that IC3D does not stock more variety with their PLA colors. I hope in the future they do so because their filament is quality as well as their packaging and customer service. I highly recommend their filament and look forward to the growth of this company.
